label: thm:harmonic
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:harmonic}
    Assume that $(M^{\mathrm{int}},g)$ is analytic and $P$ has analytic coefficients in $M$. Let $q\in L^\infty(M)$ and assume there is some open $\Sigma \subset \partial M$ that has non-empty intersection with each connected component of $M$ and assume $\partial M$ is analytic on $
    \Sigma$. If
    \[
        0 = \int_M q u_1 \overline{u_2} d V_g
    \]
    for all solutions $u_j \in C^\infty(M)$ to $P u_j = 0$ with $\mathrm{supp} u_j\vert_{\partial M}\subset \Sigma$, $j \in \{1,2\}$, then $q=0$ a.e.

label: thm:symb
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:symb}
    Let $\hat y\in \partial M$ near which $\partial M, g$ and (the coefficients of) $P$ are analytic. For any $q \in L^\infty(M)$, $\dot \Lambda_q$ is a classical analytic pseudodifferential operator of order $-1$ near $\hat y$ if and only if $q$ extends analytically across the boundary $\partial M$ near $\hat y$. In this situation it is elliptic if and only if $\lim_{M^{\mathrm{int}}\ni y\to \hat y}q(y) \neq 0$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Assume the hypotheses of \cref{thm:harmonic}, and let $q\in L^\infty(M)$ be arbitrary. If $\dot\Lambda^\Sigma_q = 0$, then $q=0$ a.e.; in other words, the map $q \mapsto \dot\Lambda^\Sigma_q$ is injective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For arbitrary $f_j \in C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$ set $u_j = Kf_j, j\in \{1,2\}$. Because $\dot\Lambda_q = -K^\ast q K$, we have
    \[
        \langle \dot\Lambda^\Sigma_q f_1, f_2 \rangle = -\int_M q u_1 \overline{u_2}\mathrm{d} V_g\,.
    \]
    In particular, if $\dot\Lambda_q^\Sigma =0$, then \cref{thm:harmonic} implies that $q=0$ a.e., completing the proof.

label: thm:lin
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:lin}
	Let $\hat y\in \partial M$ near which $\partial M, g$ and (the coefficients of) $P$ are analytic. For any open neighborhood $\Sigma\subset \partial M$ of $\hat y$, and any $q_1, q_2 \in L^\infty(M)$, if we have 
	\[
		\dot\Lambda_{q_1}^\Sigma = \dot\Lambda_{q_2}^\Sigma\,,
	\]
	then $q_1 = q_2$ a.e. near $\hat y$. 
    
    In particular, if every connected component of $M$ contains a boundary point $\in \partial M$ near which $\partial M, g$ and $P$ are analytic, and $\Sigma\subset \partial M$ is an open neighborhood of these (finitely many) boundary points, and if $q\in C^\omega(M^{\mathrm{int}})\cap L^\infty(M)$ is a potential so that $\dot\Lambda^\Sigma_q = 0$, then $q\equiv 0$ on $M$.

title: Definition
body_md:
For any $\Phi \in C(\Omega;{\mathbb{R}})$, let $\mathcal{O}^{(\Phi)}(\Omega)$ be the set of holomorphic functions $f(z;h)$ on $\Omega$ so that for all $\varepsilon>0$ and $K\subset \Omega$ compact there is $C>0$ so that for all $0<h\leq 1$
	\[
		\max_K \left\lverte^{-h^{-1}\Phi}f\right\rvert \leq C e^{h^{-1}\varepsilon}\,.
	\]
	We define the space $\mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(\Omega)$ as the set of holomorphic functions $f(z;h)$ on $\Omega$ so that for any compact $K\subset \Omega$ there are $\varepsilon,C>0$ so that for all $0<h\leq 1$,
	\[
		\max_K \left\lvertf\right\rvert \leq C e^{-h^{-1}\varepsilon}\,.
	\]
	Finally, for any $z\in \Omega$ we let $\mathbfit{O}^{(\Phi)}_z$ and $\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_z$ be the germs of these spaces at $z$.

label: def:sjostrand_Triad
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:sjostrand_Triad}
	Let $\Omega_j \subset {\mathbb{C}}^{n_j}$, $\Xi \subset {\mathbb{C}}^N$, $j\in \{1,2\}$, $\hat z \in \Omega_1$, $\hat w\in \Omega_2$, $\hat y\in \Xi$ and $\varphi \in \mathcal{O}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\times \Xi)$, and $\Phi_j \in C^\infty(\Omega_j;{\mathbb{R}})$ exponent weights so that $\varphi(\hat z, \hat w, \hat y) = 0 = \Phi_1(\hat z) = \Phi_2(\hat w)$. Define
    \[
        \Psi_1(z,w,y) = \Phi_1(z)-\varphi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(z,w,y)\,,\quad \Psi_2(z,w,y) = \Phi_2(w)+\varphi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(z,w,y)\,.
    \]

	We call $(\varphi,\Phi_1,\Phi_2)$ a \emph{Sj\"ostrand triad at $(\hat z, \hat w, \hat y)$} if
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $(\hat z, \hat y)$ is a saddle point of $\Psi_1(z,\hat w, y)$,
        \item $(\hat w, \hat y)$ is a saddle point of $\Psi_2(\hat z, w, y)$,
        \item the critical value of $(z,y)\mapsto \Psi_1(z,w,y)$ is equal to $\Phi_2(w)$ near $(\hat z, \hat w, \hat y)$.
    \end{enumerate}

label: def:sym
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:sym}
	For $m\in {\mathbb{R}}, \Omega \subset {\mathbb{C}}^n$ open and $\Gamma \subset {\mathbb{C}}^N\setminus\{0\}$ an open set conic under real dilations, when $(p_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{O}(\Omega\times \Gamma)$ is a sequence that is positively homogeneous of degree $m-j$ in $\xi\in \Gamma$ satisfying: for all compact $K\subset \Omega \times (\Gamma\cap\{\left\lvert\xi\right\rvert=1\})$ there is $C>0$ so that $\sup_K \left\lvertp_j\right\rvert \leq C^{j+1}j!$ for all $j$, we call the formal sum $\underline{p}(z,\xi) \coloneqq \sum_{j\geq 0} p_j(z,\xi)$ a \emph{formal classical analytic symbol (formal cl.a.s.) of order $m$}. 

	We say that a measurable function $p(z,\xi)$ with $p(\cdot,\xi) \in \mathcal{O}(\Omega)$ for all $\xi\in \Gamma$ is a \emph{finite realization} of $\underline{p}$ if for all sufficiently large $R>0$, for all $K\subset \Omega\times (\Gamma\cap \{\left\lvert\xi\right\rvert=1\})$ compact there are $C,\varepsilon>0$ so that for all $h \in (0,1]$,
	\[
		\sup_{(z,\xi)\in K}\left\lvertp(z,h^{-1}\xi) - \sum_{0 \leq j\leq R^{-1}h^{-1}} h^{j-m}p_j(z,\xi)\right\rvert \leq Ce^{-\varepsilon h^{-1}}\,,
	\]
	in which case we write $p\sim \underline{p}$ and say that $p$ is a \emph{classical analytic symbol (cl.a.s.).} We shall also use the notation $p(z,\xi;h)$ for $p(z,h^{-1}\xi)$ and $\underline{p}(z,\xi;h)$ for $\sum_{j\geq 0} h^{j-m}p_j(z,\xi)$ and restrict $\xi$ to a compact subset of $\Gamma$ in this case.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $U' \subset U$ be two open subsets of ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ with $\mathrm{dist}({\mathbb{R}}^n\setminus U, U') > 0$. Let $(\chi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\subset C_c^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ be a bounded sequence (in $C_c^\infty$) satisfying $0 \leq \chi_j \leq 1$ and $\chi_j\vert_{U'} \equiv 1$ and $\chi_j\vert_{{\mathbb{R}}^n\setminus U} \equiv 0$ for all $j\in \mathbb{N}$. If there is some $C>0$ so that for all multi-indices $\beta$ there is $C_\beta > 0$ so that for all $j$ we have
	\[
		\max\left\lvert\partial^\alpha \partial^\beta \chi_j\right\rvert \leq C_\beta (C j)^{\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert} \quad \forall \left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert \leq j\,,
	\]
	then $(\chi_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ is called an \emph{Ehrenpreis cut-off sequence}.

label: prop:K1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:K1}
    For fixed $\xi'_0 \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}\setminus\{0\}$, define $\psi_0(v',\tau,x') \coloneqq \frac{i}{2}(v'-x')^2+\frac{i}{2}(\tau-1)^2 - x'\cdot \xi'_0$ which is an entire function. There is a complex open neighborhood $U=U_1\times U_2$ of $((0,1),0) \in {\mathbb{C}}^{n}\times {\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ so that the following is true. For any $\chi \in C_c^\infty(U_2\cap {\mathbb{R}}^n)$ identically $1$ near $0$, for $y\in M$ and $(v',\tau)\in U_1$ and $h>0$ sufficiently small, we have
    \[
        K(\chi\vert_{\{x_n=0\}}e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0})(v',\tau,y;h) = \chi(y) e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_0(v',\tau,y)} b(v',\tau,y;h) + C^\infty(M;\mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1))\,,
    \]
    where $b(v',\tau,y;h)$ is any finite realization of some elliptic analytic symbol of order $0$ satisfying
    \[
        \mathcal{O}(U)\ni b(v',\tau,y;h) \sim \sum_{j\geq 0}h^j b_j(v',\tau,y)\,,\quad  
	(b_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{O}(U)\,,\quad b_j(v',\tau,y',0) = \delta_{0j}\,, \quad b(v',\tau,y',0)=1\,,
    \]
    where $\delta_{0j}$ is the Kronecker delta and $\phi_0 \in \mathcal{O}(U)$ satisfies 
    \[
        \phi_0(v',\tau,y',0) = \psi_0(v',\tau,y')\,,\quad (\partial_{y_n}\phi_0)(v',\tau,y) = ir^{1/2}(y,\partial_{y'}\phi_0(v',\tau,y))\,. 
    \]
    Here and in the proof below, we write $f \in C^\infty(M;\mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1))$ if $f(y,(v',\tau))\in C^\infty(M\times U_1)$ and for all $\alpha$ and all $y\in M$ we have $\partial_y^\alpha f(y, \cdot) \in \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem \cite[Thm.~9.4.6]{hoermander1}  guarantees the existence of $\phi_0$ satisfying the stated properties, i.e. it solves the eikonal equation (we use that the hypersurface $\{y_n=0\}$ is non-characteristic). 

    According to the analytic WKB method (\cite[Prop.~23.2.7]{MR4436039} or after reduction to a zero-th order equation \cite[Thm.~2.8.1]{zbMATH07060662}) there is a formal analytic symbol $\underline{b} = \sum_{j\geq 0} b_j(v',\tau,y)$ so that $P(e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_0}\underline{b}) = 0$ formally, and the $b_j$ satisfy the properties in the statement. Letting $b \sim \underline{b}$ be a finite realization satisfying the properties imposed by the statement, \cite[Prop.~24.5.2]{MR4436039} implies that 
    \[
        P(e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_0}b) \in \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U)
    \]
    if $U$ is sufficiently contracted (ie. chosen sufficiently small) about $0$.

    For $\chi$ as in the statement we define
    \[
        u = \chi e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_0}b\,, \qquad \hat u = u - GP u\,.
    \]
    One easily verifies that $\hat u\vert_{\partial M} = \chi\vert_{\{y_n=0\}} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0}$ and $P\hat u = 0$ using the properties of the Green's function $G$, so that indeed
    \[
        K(\chi\vert_{\{y_n=0\}}e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0}) = \hat u\,.
    \]
    Thus, showing that $GP u \in C^\infty(M;\mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1))$ will complete the proof. Note that
    \[
        P u = \chi P(e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_0}b) + [P,\chi]e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_0}b\,,
    \]
    where $[P,\chi]$ is supported away from $0$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have
    \[
        \phi_0(v',\tau,y) = \psi_0(v',\tau,y') + iy_n\int_0^1 r^{1/2}(y',sy_n,\partial_{y'}\phi_0(v',\tau,y',sy_n)) ds\,,
    \]
    so that $\phi_0^{i{\mathbb{R}}} > \delta > 0$ on the support of $[P,\chi]$ as long as $\left\lvert(v')^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert, \left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert$ are sufficiently small (which we can phrase as taking $U_1$ sufficiently small). Here we use the positivity of $(r^{1/2})^{{\mathbb{R}}}$.

    We conclude that $P u \in C^\infty(M; \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1))$ and the continuity of $G$ on $H^s(M), s\geq 0$ implies that $\sup_{v' \in U_1}\left\lVertGPu\right\rVert_{H^{s+2}(M)} \leq C \sup_{v' \in U_1}\left\lVertPu\right\rVert_{H^s(M)}$ with $C>0$ independent of $u$, which together with elliptic regularity (\cite[Cor.~8.3.2]{hoermander1}) gives
    \[
        GPu \in C^\infty(M; \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1))\,,
    \]
    completing the proof.

label: prop:K2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:K2}
     Let $\xi'_0 \in S^{n-2}$ be fixed, and define $\psi_1(\tau,x') = -\tau x'\cdot \xi'_0$ which is entire. There is a complex open neighborhood $U=U_1\times U_2$ of $(1,0) \in {\mathbb{C}}\times {\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ so that the following is true. For any $(\chi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}} \subset C_c^\infty(U_2)$ Ehrenpreis cut-off sequence identically $1$ near $0$ there is some complex open neighborhood $U^\ast$ of $0$ so that for all $\tau \in U_1$ and $y\in U^\ast$, and $h>0$ sufficiently small, we have
    \[
        K(\chi_{j}\vert_{\{x_n=0\}}e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1})(\tau,y;h) = e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1(\tau, y)}d(\tau,y;h) + R_j(\tau,y;h)\,,\quad \left\lvertR_j\right\rvert \leq h^m C (Cjh)^j e^{\varepsilon/h(\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert+\left\lverty^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)}
    \]
    where $\varepsilon, m \in {\mathbb{R}}, C>0$ are independent of $j$ and $R_j$ is holomorphic with respect to $(\tau, y)\in U_1\times U^\ast$, and where $d(\tau,y;h)$ is any finite realization of some elliptic classical analytic symbol of order $0$ satisfying
    \[
        \mathcal{O}(U)\ni d(\tau,y;h) \sim \sum_{j\geq 0}h^j d_j(\tau,y)\,, 
	\quad (d_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{O}(U)\,,\quad d_j(\tau,y',0) = \delta_{0,j}\,,\qquad d(\tau,y',0) = 1\,,
    \]
    and $\phi_1 \in \mathcal{O}(U)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ in $\tau$ and satisfies 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:phi}
		\phi_1(\tau, y',0) = \psi_1(\tau,y') = -\tau y'\cdot\xi'_0\,,\quad \partial_{y_n}\phi_1(\tau,y) =  ir^{1/2}(y,\partial_{y'}\phi_1(\tau,y))\,.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, there is $\vartheta_0>0$ so that for all $\vartheta \in (0,\vartheta_0]$, defining $j_\vartheta(h) \coloneqq \lfloor \vartheta h^{-1}\rfloor$, possibly contracting $U_1$ about $1$ and $U^\ast$ about $0$, we have
	\[
		K(\chi_{j_\vartheta(h)}\vert_{\{x_n=0\}}e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1})(\tau,y;h) = e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1(\tau, y)}d(\tau,y;h) + \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1\times U^\ast)\,.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the previous result, we employ the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and analytic WKB method to construct $u = \chi_{j} e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d$ and $\hat u = K(\chi_{j}\vert_{\{x_n=0\}}e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1})(\tau,y;h) = u - GPu$, and we merely have to investigate the error term $GP u$. Note again that
    \[
        Pu = \chi_{j} P(e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d) + [P,\chi_{j}]e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d\,,
    \]
    where the second term vanishes on the closed set $U_0 = \{\chi_{j}\equiv 1\forall j\}$. We assume that $U_1, U_2$ (and thus $\mathrm{supp} \chi_{j}, U_0$) are sufficiently small so that $P(e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d)\in \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1\times U_2)$. In particular, $G(\chi_{j} P(e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d))$ satisfies the bounds imposed on $R_j$ for all $j$.

    To estimate the second term above, note that for $z$ near $0$
    \[
	G([P,\chi_{j}]e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d)(z) = \int_M G(y,z) [P,\chi_{j}]e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d \mathrm{d} V_g(y)\,,
    \]
    and the kernel $G(y,z)$ of the Green's function is jointly analytic in its domain of integration. We thus perform $j$ partial integrations with the operator $L = \frac{h}{i} \frac{(\partial_{y'} \phi_1)^\ast \partial_{y'}}{\left\lvert\partial_{y'} \phi_1\right\rvert^2}$ to obtain 
    \[
	G([P,\chi_{j}]e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1}d)(z) = \int_M e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_1} (L^\ast)^j(G(y,z) [P,\chi_{j}]d)\mathrm{d} V_g(y)\,,
    \]
    which, using that $\phi_1(\tau,y',0)= -\tau y'\cdot \xi'_0$, is bounded above by $h^m C(Chj)^{j}e^{\varepsilon/h(\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert+\left\lverty^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)}$ for some $\varepsilon, C>0, m\in{\mathbb{R}}$ independent of $j$. For emphasis we point out that we have thus differentiated $\chi_j$ up to $j+2$ many times, but this merely modifies the constant $C>0$.

    Finally, choosing $\vartheta_0 = e^{-1}C^{-1}$ for the $C$ arising from the repeated partial integrations,  
    we obtain the desired exponential decay if $(\tau, y) \in U^\ast$ with complex open $U^\ast$ chosen sufficiently contracted about $0$.
	This concludes showing that for some $U^\ast$ we have $GPu \in \mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}(U_1\times U^\ast)$.

label: rem:uniformity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:uniformity}
    The construction in Proposition~\ref{prop:K2} is uniform in  near a fixed direction: for every $\xi'_{0} \in S^{n-2}$ there is a neighborhood $V \subset S^{n-2}$ of $\xi'_{0}$ such that the neighborhoods $U_1$, $U^\ast$, the constants $\varepsilon, m, C, \vartheta_0 > 0$, and the symbol $d$ can be chosen uniformly for all $\xi'_{0\ast} \in V$. This follows from continuous dependence of the construction on $\xi'_0$ as the Cauchy--Kovalevskaya solution, the transport equations, and the error estimates all depend continuously on $\xi'_0$.

label: cor:Ks
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Ks}
    Let $q\in L^\infty(M)$ and $\xi'_0 \in S^{n-2}$ be fixed. Let $\chi, (\tilde{\chi})_{j_\vartheta(h)} \in C_c^\infty(W)$ be supported sufficiently close to $0$ and identically $1$ near $0$, where $\mathrm{supp} \chi \subset \{\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)}\equiv 1\}$ and $\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)}$ is the $j_\vartheta(h)$-th element of a sequence of Ehrenpreis cut-offs as in \cref{prop:K2}. We have 
    \[
    \langle K^\ast qK\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1}, \chi e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0}\rangle = \int_M q \overline{K(\chi e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0})}K(\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1}) d V_g(y) = \int_M e^{\frac{i}{h}(-\phi_0^\ast+\phi_1)}b^\ast d \chi q \mathrm{d} V_g(y) + \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,,
    \]
    which is a function of $(v',\tau) \in {\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ defined near $(0,1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Due to \cref{prop:GK}, for any compact $V\subset U_1$, there are $C,\varepsilon>0$ so that
    \[
        \sup_{\tau \in V}\left\lVertK(\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h} \psi_1})\right\rVert_{H^2(M)} \leq C\sup_{\tau \in V}\left\lVert\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1}\right\rVert_{H^{3/2}(\partial M)} \leq Ch^{-2}\sup_{\tau \in V} e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{h} \left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert}\,,
    \]
    and we obtain from \cref{prop:K1} that, for $\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert$ sufficiently small (ie. $\tau$ sufficiently near $1$ in ${\mathbb{C}}$),  
    \[
        \int_M q \overline{K(\chi e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0})} K(\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1}) d V_g(y) = \int_M q\chi e^{-\frac{i}{h}\phi_0^\ast} b^\ast K(\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1}) d V_g(y) + \mathbfit{O}_{(0,1)}^{(-\omega)}\,.
    \]
    A similar application of \cref{prop:K2} completes the proof.

label: cor:kerndia
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the compactness of the unit sphere and homogeneity of degree $1$ of the phase $\phi_1$ (writing $h^{-1}\tau \xi'_0 = \eta'$, $h^{-1} = \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert, \left\lvert\tau\right\rvert=1$) we glue local (unique) solutions from \cref{prop:K2} together to obtain $\phi$ and $a$ as in the statement, so that
	\[
		P \left(e^{i(y'\cdot \eta'+\psi(y,\eta'))}a(y,\eta')\right) = R(y,\eta')
	\]
	where $R$ is some function that is holomorphic in $y$ near $0$ and measurable in $\eta'$ so that $\left\lvertR(y,\eta')\right\rvert \leq Ce^{-\varepsilon \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert}$ for some $C,\varepsilon>0$ and all $y$ in an open complex neighborhood of $0$. This argument required relying on \cref{rem:uniformity}. 
	
	Thus, if we define
	\[
		A(y,x') \coloneqq \int e^{i((y'-x')\cdot \eta' + \psi(y,\eta'))} a(y,\eta')\mathrm{d}\eta'\,,
	\]
	as an oscillatory integral for $y$ near $0$,  
	we have 
	\[
		P_yA(y,x') = \int e^{-ix'\cdot \eta'}R(y,\eta')\mathrm{d}\eta'\,,
	\]
	which can be holomorphically extended in $(y,x')$ near $(0,0)$ since the integrand remains absolutely integrable in $\eta'$ there.
	Similarly, because $\psi\vert_{y_n=0}=0$ and $a\vert_{y_n=0}=(2\pi)^{1-n}$, we have $A(y,x')\vert_{y_n = 0} = \delta(x'-y')$. 

	Finally, after extending $A(y,x')$ smoothly outside of the coordinate neighborhood and appealing to local analytic elliptic boundary regularity (\cite[Thm.~A]{zbMATH03134527}, applicable by reduction to zero-boundary data using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem), we deduce that $K_{a}(y,x') \coloneqq K(y,x')-A(y,x')$ is analytic in $y$ near $0$ for each fixed complex $x'$ near $0$. In fact, \cite[Thm.~2]{zbMATH03134527} states that the neighborhood of analyticity in $y$ of $K_a$ is locally uniform with respect to $x'$. 

	Note that we have, for $R' \coloneqq \int e^{-ix'\cdot\eta'}R(y,\eta')\mathrm{d}\eta' = P_yA$, writing $K_a = K-A$ and $K_a = G_yP_y K_a + K_y K_a$, and using that $K_a\vert_{y_n=0} = K - A\vert_{y_n=0}=0$, we obtain
	\[
		-K_a(\cdot, x') = G P(A-K)(\cdot,x') = GR'(\cdot,x')
	\]
	for all complex $x'$ sufficiently near $0$ (where we suppressed notation for smoothly extending functions above). Since $G, K$ are continuous linear operators with the properties stated in \cref{prop:GK}, using the Sobolev embedding, for each fixed real $y$ near $0$, and all multi-indices $\alpha$
	\[
		x' \mapsto \partial^\alpha_y K_a(y,x')
	\]
	is holomorphic in some fixed complex neighborhood of $0$ independent of $\alpha$. Using the local uniformity (with respect to $x'$) of the neighborhood on which $K_a$ is analytic in $y$, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint}
		\sup_{y \in U, x'\in V}\left\lvert\partial^\alpha_y K_a(y,x')\right\rvert \leq C R^{\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert}\alpha!\quad \forall \alpha
	\end{equation}
	for $V$ some complex neighborhood of $0$ and $U$ some real neighborhood of $0$, and $C,R>0$ some constants. In particular, for fixed $y_0 \in U$ real, 
	\[
		\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^n} \frac{\partial^\alpha_y K_a(y_0,x')}{\alpha!}(y-y_0)^\alpha
	\]
	is absolutely convergent for complex $y$ near $y_0$, and since each coefficient of this series depends holomorphically on $x'$, using \cref{eq:joint}, this series defines a holomorphic function in $(y,x')$ near $(0,0)$. Since this series agrees with $K_a(y,x')$ when $y$ is real, the proof is complete.

label: prop:anasymb
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:anasymb} 
	Let $q\in L^\infty(M)$ and assume that $\dot\Lambda_q(x',z')$ is analytic on $W'\times W'\setminus \Delta_{W'}$, where $W' \subset W$ is an open neighborhood of the origin. Let $r_0>0$ be sufficiently small and non-negative $\rho \in C^\infty(B_{r_0}(0))$ vanishing on $\left\lvertt'\right\rvert \leq r_0/2$ and identically $1$ on $B_{r_0}(0)\setminus B_{5r_0/8}(0)$. For $\gamma_\theta(t') = t'+ir_0\rho(t')\theta\left\lvert\theta\right\rvert^{-1}$, define the contour integral, for $\xi'\in {\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}\setminus\{0\}$, real $x'$ near $0$,
	\[
		\sigma_a^q(x',\xi') = - \int_{\gamma_{\xi'}(B_{r_0}(0))} e^{i(z'-x')\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(x',z')\mathrm{d} z'\,.
	\]
	For $x', z'$ sufficiently near the origin, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigma_aissymb}
		(2\pi)^{1-n}\int e^{i(x'-z')\cdot\xi'} \sigma_a^q(x',\xi') \mathrm{d} \xi' = -\dot\Lambda_q(x',z') + R(x',z')\,,
	\end{equation}
	where $R$ is analytic in a neighborhood of $(x',z')$.

	Furthermore, if $(\chi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}} \subset C_c^\infty(B_{7r_0/8}(0))$ is a sequence of Ehrenpreis cut-offs that is identically $1$ on $B_{3r_0/4}(0)$, then there is some open complex neighborhood $U$ of $(0,1)$ so that for all compact $K\subset U$ and $(x',\tau)\in K$ there are some $C,c,c'>0$ so that for all $\xi'_0\in S^{n-2}$,
	\[
		\left\lvert\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)+e^{-\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}\dot\Lambda_q(\chi_N(\cdot)e^{\frac{i}{h} \tau(\cdot)\cdot\xi'_0})(x')\right\rvert\leq C^{N+1}e^{\frac{c'}{h}(\left\lvert(x')^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert+\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)}((Nh)^N+e^{-c\tau^{\mathbb{R}} r_0/h})
	\]
	for all $N\geq 1$, and the term in the absolute value on the LHS is holomorphic with respect to $(x',\tau)$ in $U$.

label: eq:sigmaaasdistro
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\xi' = h^{-1}\tau \xi'_0$, and assume for now that $\tau=1$ and $x'$ is real near $0$. If $\beta \in C_c^\infty(B_{r_0}(0))$ is any function that is identically $1$ on $B_{5r_0/8}(0)$, the definition of $\sigma_a^q$ gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigmaaasdistro}
		-\sigma_a^q(x',\xi') = \langle \dot\Lambda_q(x',t'), \beta(t') e^{i(t'-x')\cdot \xi'} \rangle_{t'} + \int_{B_{r_0}(0)} (1-\beta(t')) e^{i(\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t')-x')\cdot\xi'} \dot\Lambda_q(x',\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t'))J_{\xi'_0}(t')\mathrm{d} t'\,,
	\end{equation}
	where the first term is a distributional pairing and the second is an ordinary integral where $J_{\theta}(t') = \mathrm{det}(\mathrm{id}+ir_0 \nabla_{t'}\rho\otimes \theta\left\lvert\theta\right\rvert^{-1})$, which is well-defined for $r_0>0$ sufficiently small because on the support of $(1-\beta)$ the kernel $\dot\Lambda_q$ has a holomorphic extension. Notice also that the second term is supported where $i\gamma_{\xi'}(t')\cdot\xi' = it' \cdot\xi' - r_0\left\lvert\xi'\right\rvert$. In particular, there is an open complex neighborhood of $0$ on which the second term has a holomorphic extension in $x'$ for all $\xi' \neq 0$ and on which the term is bounded above by $Ce^{-c\left\lvert\xi'\right\rvert}$ for some $C,c>0$. Since such exponentially decaying terms lead to analytic kernels (\cite[17.1.19]{MR4436039}), and the first term will, by ordinary Fourier inversion, lead to $-\beta(z')\dot\Lambda_q(x',z')$, the proof of \cref{eq:sigma_aissymb} is complete.

	From now on we will allow $(x',\tau)$ to be complex near $(0,1)$ so that \cref{eq:sigmaaasdistro} is seen to be the holomorphic extension of $-\sigma_{a}^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)$ in these variables. Recall that we use the notation $\xi' = h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0$.

	For $\chi_N$ as in the statement, define
	\[
		\tilde{\chi}_N(t',s) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \frac{(isr_0)^k}{k!}\left(\xi'_0\partial_{t'}\right)^k \chi_N(t')\,,
	\]
	the order $N$ almost holomorphic extension of $\chi_N$ and remark that by a telescoping property,
	\[
		\left\lvert\left(\partial_s -ir_0\xi'_0\partial_{t'}\right)\tilde{\chi}_N(t',s)\right\rvert = \left\lvert-ir_0 \frac{(isr_0)^{N-1}}{(N-1)!}\left(\xi'_0\partial_{t'}\right)^N\chi_N(t')\right\rvert  \leq C \frac{(Cr_0 N)^N}{(N-1)!} s^{N-1}\,.
	\]
	Define the integral
	\[
		I_N(x',\xi';s) \coloneqq -\int_{B_{r_0}(0)} e^{i(\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s)-x')\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(x',\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s))\tilde{\chi}_N(t',s)J_{\xi'_0}(t',s) \mathrm{d} t'\,,
	\]
	where $\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s) = t'+isr_0\rho(t')\xi'_0$ and $J_{\xi'_0}(t',s) = \det(\mathrm{id} + isr_0 \nabla_{t'}\rho(t')\otimes \xi'_0)$. We calculate that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:delsIn}
		-\partial_s I_N(x',\xi';s) = \int_{B_{r_0}(0)} e^{i(\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s)-x')\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(x',\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s))\left(\partial_s-ir_0\xi'_0\partial_{t'}\right)\tilde{\chi}_N(t',s)\mathrm{d} t'\,,
	\end{equation}
	where we used integration by parts, the identity
	\[
		\partial_s(e^{i(\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s)-x')\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(x',\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s))J_{\xi'_0}(t',s)) = ir_0\xi'_0\partial_{t'}(\rho e^{i(w'-x')\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(x',w'))\vert_{w' = \gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',s)}\,,
	\]
	and that $\rho \equiv 1$ on $\mathrm{supp} \partial_s \tilde{\chi}_N, \mathrm{supp} \nabla_{t'}\tilde{\chi}_N$. By plugging in $s=0$, we obtain
	\[
		I_N(x',\xi';0) = -e^{-ix'\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(\chi_N(\cdot)e^{i(\cdot)\cdot\xi'})(x')
	\]
	and for $s=1$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:s-1}
		\sigma_a^q(x',\xi') - I_N(x',\xi';1) = -\int_{B_{r_0}(0)} e^{i(\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',1)-x')\cdot\xi'}\dot\Lambda_q(x',\gamma_{\xi'_0}(t',1))(1-\tilde{\chi}_N(t',1))J_{\xi'_0}(t',1) \mathrm{d} t'\,.
	\end{equation}
	Notice that both integrands in \cref{eq:delsIn,eq:s-1} are supported where $t'$ is away from $0$, so that $\dot\Lambda_q$ is holomorphic where it is evaluated. In particular, writing again $\xi' = h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0$,
	\[
		\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) - I_N(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0;0) = \sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) - I_N(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0;1)+\int_0^1 \partial_s I_N(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0;s) \mathrm{d} s\,,
	\]
	is holomorphic with respect to $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$. To bound this term, we observe that (estimating $\left\lvert\tilde{\chi}_N\right\rvert\leq e^{Cr_0 N}$ and using its support properties)
	\[
		\left\lvert\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) - I_N(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0;1)\right\rvert \leq C^{N+1}e^{\frac{c'}{h}(\left\lvert(x')^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert+\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)}e^{-\frac{c}{h}r_0\tau^{{\mathbb{R}}}}
	\]
	for some $C,c,c'>0$ and 
	\[
		\int_0^1 \partial_s I_N(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0;s) \mathrm{d} s \leq e^{\frac{c'}{h}(\left\lvert(x')^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert+\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)}\int_0^1 e^{-\frac{s}{h}r_0\tau^{{\mathbb{R}}}}s^{N-1}\mathrm{d} s\frac{(Cr_0N)^N}{(N-1)!} \leq e^{\frac{c'}{h}(\left\lvert(x')^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert+\left\lvert\tau^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)}(CNh)^N\,,
	\]
	which leads to the desired estimate.

\label{thm:localmain}

Let $\chi, \tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} \in C_c^\infty(W)$ be supported sufficiently close to $0$ and identically $1$ near $0$, where $\mathrm{supp} \chi \subset \{\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)}\equiv 1\}$ and $\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)}$ is the $j_\vartheta(h)$-th element of a sequence of Ehrenpreis cut-offs as in \cref{prop:K2}. If

        \int_M q \overline{K(\chi e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_0})} K(\tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}\psi_1}) d V_g(y) \in \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,,

    then $q \equiv 0$ a.e. near $\hat y$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow the proof of \cite[Prop.~1.7]{zbMATH06600504} (in fact, see the proof of \cite[Prop.~1.5]{1312.4065v2}). Let $\chi \in C_c^\infty(W)$ have sufficiently small support and be identically $1$ near the origin. To show that $\dot \Lambda_q$ is analytic off $\Delta_{W}$ near $0$, we must prove (\cite[Thm.~22.3.15]{MR4436039}, \cite[\S~6]{AST_1982__95__R3_0}, \cite[\S~2.6]{zbMATH07060662}) that for all $v = (v_1,v_2), u= (u_1,u_2) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{2(n-1)}$ with $v_1, u_1$ near $0$ we have
	\[
		v_1\neq u_1\,, \left\lvertv_2\right\rvert+\left\lvertu_2\right\rvert = 1\implies \langle f_{v}(x')f_{u}(z'), \dot\Lambda_q(x',z') \rangle \in \mathbfit{O}_{(v_1,u_1)}^{(-\omega)}\,,
	\]
	where
	\[
		f_{v}(x') = \chi(x',0)e^{-\frac{1}{2h}(v_1-x')^2 + \frac{i}{h} x'\cdot v_2}
	\]
	and $f_u$ is defined analogously. In this proof we write $\mu(y) \mathrm{d} y$ for the measure $\mathrm{d} V_g(y)$ in the coordinate chart containing $W$, where $\mu$ is some positive analytic function. Notice first that
	\[
		-\langle f_{v}(x')f_{u}(z'), \dot\Lambda_q(x',z') \rangle = \int q \overline{Kf_v} K f_u \mathrm{d} V_g(y)\,,
	\]
	and if, for some $\varepsilon>0$, we have $\left\lvertv_2\right\rvert, \left\lvertu_2\right\rvert > \varepsilon$, then by \cref{prop:K1} (with $\tau = 1$ therein) and \cref{rem:K1imp}, we have
	\[
		\int q \overline{Kf_v} K f_u \mathrm{d} V_g(y) = \int q \chi^2 b^\ast b e^{-\frac{1}{2h}(v_1-y')^2 -\frac{1}{2h}(u_1-y')^2+ \frac{i}{h} y'\cdot (u_2-v_2) + \frac{1}{h}\mathcal{O}(y_n)} \mu(y)\mathrm{d} y + \mathbfit{O}_{(v_1,u_1)}^{(-\omega)}\,,
	\]
	where the $\mathcal{O}(y_n)$ term has non-positive real part, so that because $v_1\neq u_1$, we obtain the desired exponential decay. 

	Thus, the only case left to treat is when, say, $\left\lvertu_2\right\rvert$ is near $0$, in which case we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:someint}
		\int q \overline{Kf_v} K f_u \mathrm{d} V_g(y) = \int q \chi b^\ast e^{-\frac{1}{2h}(v_1-y')^2 - \frac{i}{h} y'\cdot v_2 + \frac{1}{h}\mathcal{O}(y_n)} Kf_u \mu\mathrm{d} y+ \mathbfit{O}_{(v_1,u_1)}^{(-\omega)}\,.
	\end{equation}
    Using local elliptic analytic boundary regularity (\cite{zbMATH03134527}), $Kf_u(y)$ is analytic in $y$ near $0$, and we write $Kf_u(y)$ also for its holomorphic extension to a complex neighborhood of $0$. One can deduce from the proof in \cite{zbMATH03134527} (or see the explicit \cite[Prop.~2.1]{zbMATH06073021}), that for sufficiently small $\delta > \delta' > 0$,
    \[
        \sup_{B_{\delta'}^{{\mathbb{C}}^n}(0)}\left\lvertKf_u\right\rvert \leq C_{\delta,\delta'} \left(\sup_{B_{\delta}^{{\mathbb{C}}^{n-1}}(0)}\left\lvertf_u\right\rvert + \left\lVertKf_u\right\rVert_{H^1(M)}\right)\,.
    \]
    By \cref{prop:GK}, the second term on the RHS above can be be bounded by $\left\lVertf_u\right\rVert_{H^{3/2}(\partial M)} \lesssim C h^m$ for some $m>0$, and by choosing $\delta>0$ small and estimating $f_u$ directly, we obtain 
    \[
        \sup_{B_{\delta'}^{{\mathbb{C}}^n}(0)}\left\lvertKf_u\right\rvert \leq e^{c(\delta^2+\delta\left\lvertu_2\right\rvert)/h}
    \]
    for some $C,c>0$.

	Introduce a sequence of Ehrenpreis cut-offs $(\chi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}} \subset C_c^\infty(\{\chi \equiv 1\})$ and identically $1$ near $0$. Split the integral on the RHS of \cref{eq:someint} into two terms corresponding to $\chi = \chi_N + \chi (1-\chi_N)$. The term containing the cut-offs $\chi (1-\chi_N)$ is supported away from the origin, so that the Gaussian factor $e^{-\frac{1}{2h}(v_1-y')^2}$ induces exponential decay if $v_1$ and $\left\lvertu_2\right\rvert$ and $\delta>0$ are sufficiently near $0$ (so that the bound $Ce^{c(\delta^2+\delta\left\lvertu_2\right\rvert)/h}$ for the absolute value of the holomorphic extension of $Kf_u(y)$ is negligible). Thus, we must only estimate 
	\[
		\int q \chi_N b^\ast e^{-\frac{1}{2h}(v_1-y')^2 - \frac{i}{h} y'\cdot v_2 + \frac{1}{h}\mathcal{O}(y_n)} Kf_u \mathrm{d} y\,,
	\]
	for which we rely on repeated partial integrations and the fact that $\left\lvertv_2\right\rvert > \varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ and $q$ is analytic near $0$. After $N$ repeated partial integrations, using the Cauchy inequalities, one obtains a bound of the form $(Ch N/\delta)^N e^{c(\delta^2+\delta\left\lvertu_2\right\rvert)/h}$, so that assuming $\delta, \left\lvertu_2\right\rvert>0$ are sufficiently small and taking $N = N(h) = \lfloor \vartheta h^{-1} \rfloor$ for some $\vartheta>0$ sufficiently small leads to the desired exponential decay. 

	We have completed the proof of the fact that $\dot\Lambda_q$ is analytic off the diagonal near $0$. We shall prove that $\sigma_a^q(x',\xi')$ is a cl.a.s. of order $-1$ with fiber variable $\xi' \in {\mathbb{C}}^{n-1}\setminus\{0\}$, for which we shall pass to the semi-classical realm: write $\xi' = h^{-1} \tau \xi'_0, \left\lvert\xi'_0\right\rvert=1$, with complex $\tau$ near 1. Again, let $(\chi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of Ehrenpreis cut-offs identically $1$ near the origin and choose $j_\vartheta(h)$ according to \cref{prop:K2} so that
	\[
		K(\chi_{j_\vartheta(h)} e^{\frac{i}{h}
        \tau(\cdot)\cdot\xi'_0}) = e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi(\tau,y,\xi'_0)} a(y,h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) + \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,,
	\]
	where the glued solutions $a, \phi$ are from \cref{cor:kerndia}.
	Using the analytic WKB method to solve an inhomogeneous equation (\cite[Thm.~2.8.1]{zbMATH07060662}), there is a cl.a.s. $f$ of order $-1$ with $f\vert_{x_n=0}=0$ so that modulo a term in $\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{0} \subset \mathbfit{O}^{(0)}_{0}$, for $x$ near $0$,
	\[
		G(q e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi}a)(x) = f(x,h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi(\tau,x,\xi'_0)}\,.
	\]
	Notice also that by the same argument $G(\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}) = \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}$ so that differentiating once in $y_n$, multiplying by $e^{- \frac{i}{h} \tau x'\cdot \xi'_0}$ and evaluating at $x_n=0$ gives that $e^{-\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}\dot\Lambda_q(\chi_{j_\vartheta(h)}(\cdot)e^{\frac{i}{h}\tau (\cdot)\cdot\xi'_0})(x')$ is a cl.a.s. (recall $K = \partial_{x_n} G \vert_{x_n=0}$). However, by \cref{prop:anasymb}, this property (recall the `optimal' choice of $j=j_\vartheta(h)$ makes the error in this reference exponentially decaying for $\vartheta>0$ sufficiently small) is true also for $\sigma_a^q$, completing this proof.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:symbcalc}
    For all $x'$ sufficiently near $\hat y = 0$ in $W$, for $\chi \in C_c^\infty(W)$ identically $1$ near $0$ with sufficiently small support and any $\xi' \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}\setminus\{0\}$ we define, for $a, \psi$ from \cref{cor:kerndia} and $q\in L^\infty(M)$, 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:definesigma}
        \sigma_b^q(x',\xi') \coloneqq (2\pi)^{n-1}\iint e^{i(x'-y')\cdot(\eta'-\xi')}e^{i(\psi(y,\xi')-\psi^\ast(y,\eta'))}a(y,\xi') a^\ast(y,\eta')\mathrm{d}\eta' \chi(y)q(y) \mu(y)\mathrm{d} y\,,
    \end{equation}
    where $\mu(y) \mathrm{d} y$ is the measure $\mathrm{d} V_g(y)$ in the coordinate chart containing $W$, notation we shall suppress in $\sigma_b^q$ from hereon out (one may subsume $\mu$ into $q$, say). 

	Let $\tilde{q}\in C_c^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ be analytic near the origin, $\xi'_0\in S^{n-2}$ fixed. We have
	\[
		\left(\sigma_a^{1_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}- \sigma_b^{1_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}\right)(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) = \mathcal{O}(h^\infty)
	\]
	uniformly for real $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$.

label: eq:eq
title: Proof
body_md:
Use \cref{cor:kerndia} to obtain, if $x'$ near $\hat y$ and the support of $\chi$ is sufficiently small,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:eq}
        \sigma_b^q(x',\xi') =  
        (2\pi)^{n-1}\int \overline{(K(y,x')-K_a(y,x'))}\chi(y)q(y) e^{i(y'-x')\cdot \xi' + i\psi(y,\xi')}a(y,\xi') \mathrm{d} y\,.
    \end{equation}

	For $(\tilde{\chi}_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ an Ehrenpreis cut-off sequence identically $1$ and supported near $0$, define
	\[
		g_{N,\tau,h}(z') = \chi_{N}(z')e^{\frac{i}{h}\tau z'\cdot\xi'_0}\,. 
	\]
	According to \cref{prop:anasymb} we have
	\[
		\sigma_a^{1_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) = e^{-\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}K^\ast \tilde{q}K(g_{N,\tau,h}) + \mathcal{O}_N(h^N)\,.
	\]
	According to \cref{eq:eq}, we have 
	\[
		\sigma_b^{1_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) = e^{-\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}(K^\ast-K_a^\ast)(\chi \tilde{q} K g_{N,\tau,h} + \mathcal{O}_N(h^N))\,.
	\]
	Using the continuity of $K$ on Sobolev spaces (and directly estimating $K_a$) we obtain, for some fixed $m>0$,
	\[
		(\sigma_a - \sigma_b)^{1_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) = e^{-\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}(B_1+B_2)g_{N,\tau,h} + \mathcal{O}_N(h^{N-m})\,,
	\]
	where
	\[
		B_1 = K^\ast (1-\chi) \tilde{q} K\,,\qquad B_2 = K_a^\ast \chi \tilde{q} K= K^\ast(\overline{K_a(\cdot,x')}\chi(\cdot)\tilde{q}(\cdot))\,.
	\]
	Since $K_a$ is smooth near the origin, if $\chi$ is supported sufficiently close to the origin, $B_2$ is seen to be a smooth function for each fixed $x'$. Since it also depends smoothly on $x'$, the kernel $B_2$ is smooth in a neighborhood of the origin. That $B_1$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the origin follows from the fact that when $(x',z')$ near the origin, then $y\in \mathrm{supp}(1-\chi)$ is separated from $x',z'$. 

	Finally, by applying repeated partial integrations, one sees that $(B_1+B_2)g_{N,\tau,h} = \mathcal{O}_N(h^{N-m'})$ for some $m'>0$ (independent of $N$), so that in total, taking $N$ sufficiently large the proof is complete.

\label{lem:phi3props}

    \[
        \phi_2(w,y) \coloneqq -\phi^\ast_0(v',\tau,y) + \phi_1(\tau,y)

Starting at the top-left and going clockwise, these blocks are with respect to $\partial_{y'}\partial_{v'}$, $\partial_{y'}\partial_{\tau}$, $\partial_{y_n}\partial_{v'}$, and $\partial_{y_n}\partial_{\tau}$. 
	\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by showing that 
\[
	\Psi_1(z,x) \coloneqq \Phi^\sharp(z)-\phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(z,\hat w, x)
\]
has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and that $\phi_4(0,(0,1),0) = 0 = \Phi^\sharp(0)$, the latter part being true by explicit computation.

\textbf{First order:} Note first that
\[
	-\partial_x\Psi_1(0,0) = \partial_x \phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}} = \frac{1}{2i}\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}(\phi_2-\hat\phi) = 0\,,
\]
and $\partial_z \Phi^\sharp = 0$ and $\partial_z \phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}}=0$ which gives $\partial_z\Psi_1 = 0$. Thus, indeed $\partial_{(z,x)} \Psi_1 (0,0) = 0$.

\textbf{Second order:} Notice that  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hesspsi1}
	M \coloneqq \partial_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},x^{\mathbb{R}},z^{i{\mathbb{R}}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}^2\Psi_1 = \begin{pmatrix}A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}+B& A^{{\mathbb{R}}} \\ A^{{\mathbb{R}}} & -A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\end{pmatrix}\,, 
\end{equation}
where starting from the top-left and going clockwise the blocks are given by $\partial^2_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},x^{\mathbb{R}})}$, $\partial_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},x^{\mathbb{R}})}\partial_{(z^{i{\mathbb{R}}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}$, $\partial_{(z^{i{\mathbb{R}}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}\partial_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},x^{\mathbb{R}})}$, and $\partial^2_{(z^{i{\mathbb{R}}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hesspsi1AB}
	 A \coloneqq -\partial_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},x^{\mathbb{R}})}^2\phi_4\,,\quad B \coloneqq \begin{pmatrix}\hat c\mathrm{id}_{(n-1)} & 0 \\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix}\,.
\end{equation}
We calculate that
\[
	A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -i\hat c\mathrm{id} \\ -i\hat c\mathrm{id} & i\hat c\mathrm{id}-\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2\end{pmatrix}\,,
\]
which is invertible and note that
\[
	A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}+ B = \begin{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\hat c\mathrm{id}_{(n-1)} & 0 \\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix} & -\hat c\mathrm{id} \\ -\hat c\mathrm{id} & \hat c\mathrm{id} - \partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\end{pmatrix}\,.
\]
Using that $A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}$ is invertible by explicit computation, Sylvester's law of inertia, or the Haynsworth inertia additivity formula imply that 
\[
	\mathrm{sign}(M) = \mathrm{sign}(-A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}) + \mathrm{sign}(A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}+B-A^{\mathbb{R}}(-A^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1} A^{\mathbb{R}})\,.
\]
Because $A^{\mathbb{R}} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{{\mathbb{R}}}\end{pmatrix}$, by explicit computation we find that $A^{\mathbb{R}}(-A^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1} A^{\mathbb{R}} = 0$ so that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:signM}
		\mathrm{sign}(M) = \mathrm{sign}(-A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}) + \mathrm{sign}(A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}+B)\,.
	\end{equation}
Using Haynsworth's formula,
\[
	\mathrm{sign}(A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}+B) = \mathrm{sign}(\hat c\mathrm{id}-\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_2) + \mathrm{sign}\left(\begin{pmatrix}\hat c\mathrm{id}_{(n-1)} & 0 \\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix}-\hat c^2 (\hat c \mathrm{id} -\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1}\right)\,.
\]
First, if $\hat c>0$ is sufficiently large, the first term on the RHS is $(n,0)$. Second,  
using Neumann series, 
\[
	-\hat c^2 (\hat c \mathrm{id} -\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1}=-\hat c\mathrm{id} - \partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}} + \mathcal{O}(\hat c^{-1})\,,
\]
so that 
\begin{align*}
	\begin{pmatrix}\hat c\mathrm{id}_{(n-1)} & 0 \\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix}&-\hat c^2 (\hat c \mathrm{id} -\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}0& 0 \\ 0&-\hat c \end{pmatrix} - \partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}} + \mathcal{O}(\hat c^{-1}) = \begin{pmatrix}-\mathrm{id}& * \\ * & -\hat c+ * \end{pmatrix} + \mathcal{O}(\hat c^{-1})\,,
\end{align*}
by the explicit formula for $\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}}$ calculated in \cref{lem:phi3props}, and where $*$ is a term we do not compute but that is independent of $\hat c$. Using Haynsworth's formula, we find that the signature of the first matrix on the RHS is 
\[
	\mathrm{sign}(-\mathrm{id}) + \mathrm{sign}(-\hat c + *)\,,
\]
which is $(0,n)$ for $\hat c>0$ sufficiently large. In particular, we have for sufficiently large $\hat c>0$ that $\mathrm{sign}(\begin{pmatrix}\hat c\mathrm{id}_{(n-1)} & 0 \\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix}-\hat c^2 (\hat c \mathrm{id} -\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1}) = (0,n)$, and thus we conclude that $\mathrm{sign}(A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}+B)=(n,n)$.

The same type of arguments (but simpler) lead to 
\[
	\mathrm{sign}(A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}) = \mathrm{sign}(\hat c\mathrm{id}-\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}}) + \mathrm{sign}(- \hat c^2(\hat c\mathrm{id} -\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}^2\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}})^{-1})\,,
\]
where taking $\hat c>0$ large enough yields that $A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}$ (and thus also $-A^{i{\mathbb{R}}}$) has signature $(n,n)$.

By \cref{eq:signM}, this implies that the matrix in \cref{eq:hesspsi1} has signature $(2n,2n)$ (and thus is non-degenerate) so that we have the desired saddle point of $\Psi_1$.  


\textbf{The `dual' exponent weight:}

Introduce $\Phi^{\sharp,\ast}(w) = (\Phi^\sharp-\phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}})(z(w),w,x(w))$, where $(z(w),x(w))$ is defined by $\partial_{(z,x)}(\Phi^\sharp-\phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}})(z,w,x) = 0\iff (z,x)=(z(w),x(w))$. Note also that $\Phi^{\sharp,\ast}(\hat w)=0$.

If we show that 
\[
	\Psi_2(w,x) \coloneqq \Phi^{\sharp,\ast}(w)+\phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(\hat z, w, x)
\]
has a saddle point at $(\hat w, \hat x) = ((0,1),0)$, then by our choice of $\Phi^{\sharp,\ast}$ we will have completed the proof of the fact that $(\phi_4,\Phi^\sharp,\Phi^{\sharp,\ast})$ is a Sj\"ostrand triad at $(0,(0,1),0)$. 

\textbf{First order:} By \cref{lem:phi3props},
\[
	\partial_{w}\Phi^{\sharp,\ast}(\hat w) = -\partial_{w}\phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(\hat z, \hat w, \hat x) = -\partial_{w}\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(\hat w, \hat x) = 0 = \partial_w\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_4(\hat z,\hat w,\hat x)\,, 
\]
so that $\partial_w \Psi_2(\hat w, \hat x) =0$. Furthermore, by explicit calculation $\partial_{x}\Psi_2(\hat w,\hat x) = \partial_{x}\Psi_1(\hat w, \hat x) = 0$ so that we have the desired critical point at $(\hat w, \hat x)$.

\textbf{Second order:} denote $A_{u,v} \coloneqq \partial_{(u^{\mathbb{R}},u^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}\partial_{(v^{\mathbb{R}},v^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}(\Phi^\sharp -\phi_4^{i{\mathbb{R}}})(0,(0,1),0)$ for $u,v \in \{w,z,x\}$ and $\tilde{M} \coloneqq \partial^2_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},z^{i{\mathbb{R}}},x^{{\mathbb{R}}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}\Psi_1(0,0)$, which is a reordering of the matrix $M$ in \cref{eq:hesspsi1}:
\[
	\tilde{M} \coloneqq \begin{pmatrix}M_1 & M_2 \\ M_3 & M_4\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\text{where}\quad M_4 = \partial_{(x^{\mathbb{R}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}^2(-\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_4)(0,(0,1),0) = \begin{pmatrix}\hat c\mathrm{id} & 0 \\ 0&-\hat c\mathrm{id}\end{pmatrix} + \partial_{(x^{\mathbb{R}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}^2(-\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_2)(0,(0,1),0)\,.
\]
In particular, for sufficiently large $\hat c>0$, the signature of $M_4$ is $(n,n)$ which also implies that it is non-degenerate. Furthermore, we had already computed that $M$ has signature $(2n,2n)$ (and thus $\tilde{M}$ has signature $(2n,2n)$ by Sylvester's law of inertia) so that the Haynsworth formula tells us that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:signZ}
	\mathrm{sign}(M_1 - M_2M_4^{-1}M_3) = (n,n)\,.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, as a consequence of the implicit function theorem, we have
\[
	\partial_{(w^{\mathbb{R}},w^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}^2\Phi^{\sharp,\ast}(0,(0,1)) = A_{w,w} - A_{w,(z,x)}\tilde{M}^{-1}A_{w,(z,x)}^T\,,
\]
and in particular,
\[
	W \coloneqq \partial_{(w^{{\mathbb{R}}},w^{i{\mathbb{R}}},x^{{\mathbb{R}}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}^2 \Psi_2((0,1),0) = \begin{pmatrix} - A_{w,(z,x)}\tilde{M}^{-1}A_{w,(z,x)}^T & -A_{w,x} \\ -A_{w,x}^T & -A_{x,x}\end{pmatrix}\,.
\]
Note that $A_{x,x} = M_4$, so that we can use Haynsworth's formula to calculate that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:signW}
	\mathrm{sign}(W) = \mathrm{sign}(-M_4) + \mathrm{sign}(- A_{w,(z,x)}\tilde{M}^{-1}A_{w,(z,x)}^T + A_{w,x}M_4^{-1} A_{w,x}^T)\,.
\end{equation}
Defining $Z = (A_{z,z}-A_{z,x}A_{x,x}^{-1}A_{x,z})^{-1} = (M_1 - M_2M_4^{-1}M_3)^{-1}$ (which has signature $(n,n)$ due to \cref{eq:signZ}),
\[
	\tilde{M}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}Z & -ZM_2M_4^{-1} \\ -M_4^{-1}M_3Z & M_4^{-1}+M_4^{-1}M_3ZM_2M_4^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\,,
\]
and by explicit computation we find that for $V \coloneqq A_{w,z}-A_{w,x}A_{x,x}^{-1}A_{x,z}$,
\[
	- A_{w,(z,x)}\tilde{M}^{-1}A_{w,(z,x)}^T + A_{w,x}M_4^{-1} A_{w,x}^T = -VZV^T\,.
\]
In particular, if $V$ is non-degenerate, then Sylvester's law of inertia says that $\mathrm{sign}(-VZV^T) = \mathrm{sign}(-Z) = (n,n)$. Therefore, showing that $V$ is non-degenerate will imply that $\mathrm{sign}(W) = (2n,2n)$ by \cref{eq:signW}. 

Now notice that $A_{w,z} = 0$ and $A_{x,z} = -\partial_{(x^{\mathbb{R}},x^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}\partial_{(z^{\mathbb{R}},z^{i{\mathbb{R}}})}\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_4 = \begin{pmatrix}-\hat c \mathrm{id} & 0 \\ 0 & \hat c\mathrm{id}\end{pmatrix}$, which is invertible. In particular, $V$ is non-degenerate if and only if $A_{w,x}$ is non-degenerate, and 
\[
	A_{w,x} = -\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{B}^{i{\mathbb{R}}} & \tilde{B}^{\mathbb{R}} \\ \tilde{B}^{\mathbb{R}} & -\tilde{B}^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\text{with}\quad \tilde{B} = \partial_{w^{\mathbb{R}}}\partial_{x^{\mathbb{R}}}\phi_4 = -\begin{pmatrix}i\mathrm{id} & \xi'_0 \\ -(\partial_{\eta'}r^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0))^T & -ir^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0)\end{pmatrix}^T \,,
\]
where the Schur complement test implies that $A_{w,x}$ is non-degenerate. Thus, we have verified that $\Psi_2$ has the desired saddle point. 

In particular, by the definition of $\Phi^{\sharp,\ast}$, we have indeed verified that $(\phi_4, \Phi^\sharp, \Phi^{\sharp,\ast})$ is a Sj\"ostrand triad at $(\hat z, \hat w, \hat x)$.

Finally, we calculate that 
\[
	 \begin{pmatrix}\partial_z\partial_w\phi_4 & \partial_z\partial_x \phi_4 \\ \partial_w\partial_x\phi_4 & \partial_x^2\phi_4\end{pmatrix} =  \begin{pmatrix}0 & i\hat c\mathrm{id} \\ \partial_w\partial_x\phi_4 & \partial_x^2\phi_4\end{pmatrix}\,,
\]
which is non-degenerate if and only if
\[
	\partial_w\partial_x\phi_4 = \partial_w\partial_x\phi_2
\]
is non-degenerate, which it is. This completes the proof.

label: eq:contcalc
title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify \eqref{eq:f_neg_def}. By the definitions of $\hat\phi, \Phi^\sharp$ we have
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:contcalc}
        \hat \phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(\bar x, x) = -\frac{\hat c}{2}\left\lvertx^{\mathbb{R}}\right\rvert^2 - \frac{3\hat c}{2}\left\lvertx^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert^2+2r_0 x_n^{\mathbb{R}}\,, \quad \Phi^\sharp(\bar x) = \frac{\hat c}{2}\left\lvert(x^{\mathbb{R}})'\right\rvert^2\,,
    \end{equation}
    and by the properties of $\phi_2$ (\cref{lem:phi3props}) and Taylor's theorem, with $M = \partial_y^2 \phi_2(\hat w,0)$,
    \[
        -\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_2(\hat w, x) = -2r_0x_n^{\mathbb{R}} - \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Im}(x^TMx)+\mathcal{O}(\left\lvertx\right\rvert^3)\,,\quad \mathrm{Im}(x^TMx) \geq \left\lvert(x^{\mathbb{R}})'\right\rvert^2 - 2C_M(\left\lvert(x^{\mathbb{R}})'\right\rvert(\left\lvertx^{\mathbb{R}}_n\right\rvert+\left\lvertx^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert)+\left\lvertx_n^{\mathbb{R}}\right\rvert^2+\left\lvertx^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert^2)
    \]
    for some $C_M>0$ depending only on $M$. Thus,
    \[
        \Psi_1(\bar x, x) \leq -\frac{1}{2}\left\lvert(x^{\mathbb{R}})'\right\rvert^2 + C_M\left\lvert(x^{\mathbb{R}})'\right\rvert(\left\lvertx^{\mathbb{R}}_n\right\rvert+\left\lvertx^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert) - \left(\frac{\hat c}{2}-C_M\right)(\left\lvertx_n^{\mathbb{R}}\right\rvert^2+\left\lvertx^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert^2) - \frac{\hat c}{2}\left\lvertx^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert^2 + \mathcal{O}(\left\lvertx\right\rvert^3)\,,
    \]
    so that for $\hat c>0$ sufficiently large, the quadratic form (on $x$) on the RHS is negative definite. In particular, there is some $c_\psi>0$ so that $\Psi_1(\bar x, x) \leq -c_\psi\left\lvertx\right\rvert^2 = -c_\psi (\left\lvert\bar x\right\rvert^2+\left\lvertx\right\rvert^2)/2$ on $\mathfrak{C}_{\rho/2}$ for small $\rho>0$. Since $\Psi_1(0,0)=0$ the proof of part 1. is complete.

    We introduce $\zeta = -i\hat c z$ and $E(x;h) \coloneqq e^{-\frac{1}{h}(\frac{\hat c}{2}x\cdot x+2r_0x_n)}$ which is a non-vanishing entire function. By \cref{eq:defhatphi},
    \[
        e^{\frac{i}{h}(\hat \phi(z,y)-\hat\phi(z,x))} = e^{\frac{i}{h}(y-x)\cdot \zeta}E(y;h)E(x;h)^{-1}\,,
    \]
    and after the change of variables $z\mapsto \zeta$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:germpsido}
        \int_{\mathfrak{C}_{\rho/2}} e^{\frac{i}{h}(\hat \phi(z,y)-\hat\phi(z,x))} g(x;h) \mathrm{d} z\mathrm{d} x = c_1E(y;h)\int_{\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\rho/2}}e^{\frac{i}{h}(y-x)\cdot \zeta}g(x;h)E(x;h)^{-1}\mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} \zeta\,,
    \end{equation}
    where $c_1$ is a non-vanishing constant depending only on $n$ and $\hat c$ and $\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_\rho = \{(x,-i\hat c\bar x)\colon \left\lvertx\right\rvert<\rho\}$. The integral on the RHS is \cite[Eq.~(21.1.2)]{MR4436039} with symbol identically $1$, output variable $y$ and input $g E^{-1}\in \mathcal{O}^{(\Phi_E)}(B_\rho)$, where 
    \[
        \Phi_E(x) \coloneqq \Phi(x)+\frac{\hat c}{2}\mathrm{Re}(x\cdot x)+2r_0x_n^{\mathbb{R}}\,.
    \]
    Observe that $\Phi_E(0)=0, \partial_x\Phi_E(0) = 0$, and the Hessian of $\Phi_E$ is $\hat c \mathrm{diag}(\mathrm{id}, -\mathrm{id}) + \mathcal{O}(1)$ which is non-degenerate of signature $(n,n)$ for $\hat c>0$ large enough. In particular, $0$ is a saddle point of $\Phi_E$ and on $\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_\rho$, by \cref{eq:contcalc},
    \[
        \Phi_E(x) - \mathrm{Im}((0-x)\cdot \zeta) = \Phi_E(x) -\hat c \left\lvertx\right\rvert^2 = \Psi_1(\bar x, x)- \frac{\hat c}{2}\left\lvert(x^{\mathbb{R}})'\right\rvert^2 \leq -c_\psi\left\lvertx\right\rvert^2\,,
    \]
    so that $\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_\rho$ is a strongly well-shaped contour for $\Phi_E(x) - \mathrm{Im}((0-x)\cdot \zeta)$ at $(0,0)$. This verifies the hypotheses of \cite[Thm.~21.1.2]{MR4436039} so that the integral on the RHS of \cref{eq:germpsido} is a germ pseudo-differential operator on $\mathcal{O}^{(\Phi_E)}_0/\mathcal{O}^{(-\omega)}_0$ with symbol $1$, which is the identity by \cite[Cor.~21.1.8]{MR4436039} (using the independence with respect to the contour \cite[Rem.~21.1.9]{MR4436039}). We obtain the first part of statement 2. 

    The quantitative part of statement 2. is obtained by tracing that \cite[Prop.~20.2.14]{MR4436039} is stated with an error bound $Ce^{-\kappa/h}\sup_{K}e^{-\Phi_E/h}\left\lvertgE^{-1}(\cdot;h)\right\rvert$ for some $C,\kappa>0$, and (the proofs of) \cite[Thm.~21.1.7,~Prop.~20.4.3,~Prop.20.4.8]{MR4436039} bound error terms by $C\sup_{K}e^{-\Phi_E/h}\left\lvertg E^{-1}\right\rvert$ for some compact $K\Subset B_\rho$ containing all contours involved, uniformly in $y$ near $0$. Because $e^{-\Phi_E/h}\left\lvertg E^{-1}\right\rvert = e^{-\Phi/h}\left\lvertg\right\rvert$ and $\left\lvertE(y;h)\right\rvert\leq e^{C\left\lverty\right\rvert/h}$ for some $C>0$, after shrinking $U$ the proof is complete. (Note that the standing assumption of \cite[\S~21.1.3]{MR4436039} that $\partial_x\Phi_E(0) \neq 0$ is not used in the proofs of the results cited here.)

title: Proof
body_md:
\cref{lem:contour} implies that $\mathcal{T}$ is well-defined (\cite[Thm.~20.5.6,~Def.~20.5.7]{MR4436039}). By \cref{lem:tdTinvnew}, $(\phi_4,\Phi^\sharp, \Phi^{\sharp,\ast})$ is a Sj\"ostrand triad at $(0,\hat w, 0)$, and the same lemma gives the hypotheses of \cite[Thm.~21.2.12]{MR4436039}, which completes the proof of the first part. 

    Define $g_w(x;h)\coloneqq e^{\frac{i}{h}\phi_2(w,x)}b^\ast(w,x;h)d(w_n,x;h)$ which is holomorphic on $B_\rho$ for $w$ near $\hat w$ provided $\rho$ is sufficiently small. Using Fubini's theorem
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:fub}
        \mathcal{T}_\rho (Au)(w;h) = c_h^{-1}\int u(y) \int_{\mathfrak{C}_{\rho/2}}e^{\frac{i}{h}(\hat \phi(z,y)-\hat \phi(z,x))}g_w(x;h)\mathrm{d} z \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y\,.
    \end{equation}
    Because $b^\ast d = \mathcal{O}(h^0)$ near $(\hat w,0)$, we obtain
    \[
        \left\lvertg_w(x;h)\right\rvert \leq Ce^{(\Phi(x)+L\left\lvertw-\hat w\right\rvert)/h}
    \]
    for $x\in B_\rho$ and $w$ near $\hat w$, $\Phi(x) = -\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}_2(\hat w,x)$ and $L$ a Lipschitz constant of $\phi_2^{i{\mathbb{R}}}$ in $w$. We find that \cref{lem:contour} implies that the inner contour integral in the RHS of \cref{eq:fub} evaluates to $c_hg_w(y;h)+R_w(y;h)$ with $\sup_{y\in U}\left\lvertR_w(y)\right\rvert\leq Ch^{-n}e^{(-\varepsilon+L\left\lvertw-\hat w\right\rvert)/h}$. If $\mathrm{supp} u \subset U$, then by \cref{eq:defofS}, 
    \[
        \mathcal{T}_\rho (Au)(w;h) = \int u(y)g_w(y;h)\mathrm{d} y+ c_h^{-1}\int u(y)R_w(y;h)\mathrm{d} y = Su(w;h)+\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{\hat w}
    \]
    if we choose $\left\lvertw-\hat w\right\rvert< \varepsilon/(2L)$, since $\mathcal{T}_\rho (Au)(w;h)$ and $Su(w;h)$ are holomorphic in $w$ near $\hat w$.

label: lem:phiflat
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:phiflat}
	Define 
	\[
		\Phi^\flat(z) \coloneqq \sup_{{\mathbb{R}}^n\ni y, y_n\geq 0}-\hat\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(z,y) 	
	\]
	which is continuous on ${\mathbb{C}}^n$ and satisfies
	\[
			\Phi^\flat(z) = \frac{\hat c}{2}((z')^{{\mathbb{R}}})^2 + \begin{cases}\hat c/2(z_n^{\mathbb{R}}-2\hat c^{-1}r^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0))^2&\quad\text{if}\ z_n^{\mathbb{R}} \geq 2\hat c^{-1}r^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0) \\ 0 &\quad\text{if}\ z_n^{\mathbb{R}} < 2\hat c^{-1}r^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0)\end{cases}\,.
	\]
	Furthermore, $\hat\phi$ is an FBI phase function at $(z^\circ_\nu,0), z^\circ_\nu = i\hat c^{-1}\hat\xi + i\nu e_n$, where $e_n$ is the $n$-th standard basis vector and $\nu > 0$ is arbitrary, with $\partial_y\hat\phi(z^\circ_\nu,0)=\hat c\nu e_n$.

	In particular, $A \colon L_{c,+}^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n)\to \mathcal{O}^{(\Phi^\flat)}({\mathbb{C}}^n)$ is continuous (without any germ restriction).

title: Proof
body_md:
For $y$ real,
\[
	-\hat\phi^{i{\mathbb{R}}}(z,y) = -{\hat c\over 2}y^2 +\hat cz^{\mathbb{R}} \cdot y - 2r^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0)y_n\,,
\]
for which one can explicitly see that the supremum in the definition of $\Phi^\flat$ is attained and can be computed explicitly as stated. To verify that $A$ is a germ FBI transform at $(z^\circ_\nu,0)$ we must only check that $\hat \phi$ is an FBI phase function at $(z^\circ_\nu,0)$: 
\[
	\hat\phi(z^\circ_\nu,0) = 0\,, \partial_y\hat\phi(z^\circ_\nu,0) = \hat c\nu e_n\,, \det\partial_z\partial_y\hat\phi(z^\circ_\nu,0) = (-i \hat c)^n \neq 0\,, \mathrm{Im}\partial_y\partial_y\hat\phi(z^\circ_\nu,0) = \hat c\mathrm{id} > 0\,.
\]
A minor modification of \cite[Prop.~22.2.7]{MR4436039} to reflect the additional assumption that if an input function is supported in $\{y_n\geq 0\}$, we may define $\Phi^\flat$ by taking the supremum over $y_n\geq 0$, the proof is complete.

body_md: Let $\rho\in (0,\rho_0]$ with $\rho_0>0$ sufficiently small from \cref{lem:contour}. Inverting $\mathcal{T}$, we find that $Au = 0$ in $\mathbfit{O}_{0}^{(\Phi^\sharp)}/\mathbfit{O}_{0}^{(-\omega)}$, which is to say that $Au \in \mathbfit{O}_{0}^{(-\omega)}$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:complexshift}
	If $u\in L^\infty_{c,+}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ with $Su\in\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}$ has support sufficiently contracted about $0$, then for $\nu>0$ sufficiently small,
	\[
		Au = 0 \quad\text{in}\ \mathbfit{O}^{(\Phi^\flat)}_{z^\circ_\nu}/\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{z^\circ_\nu}\,.
	\]

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\nu >0$ sufficiently small (as will be chosen throughout this proof) writing $z^\circ = z^\circ_\nu$, let us define
\[
	\Phi^{\flat,\circ}(z)\coloneqq \Phi^\flat(z+z^\circ) = \frac{\hat c}{2}((z')^{{\mathbb{R}}})^2  + \begin{cases}\frac{\hat c}{2}(z_n^{\mathbb{R}})^2 \quad&\text{if}\ z_n^{\mathbb{R}}\geq 0\\ 0\quad&\text{else}\end{cases}\,,
\]
where we used that $\hat \xi= -(0, 2ir^{1/2}(0,\xi'_0))$. Our assumptions and \cref{lem:fbifirst} imply
\[
	A^\circ u(z) \coloneqq Au(\cdot + z^\circ) \in \mathcal{O}^{(\Phi^{\flat,\circ})}({\mathbb{C}}^n)\,,\quad\text{and}\quad A^\circ u(z)\in \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{-z^\circ}\,,
\]
and the proof is complete if we show that $A^\circ u \in \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{0}$. We give $z_n$ a distinguished role and thus define, for some $\varepsilon^\circ >0$ sufficiently small and some sufficiently large constant $C>0$ independent of $h$,
\[
	F(z', z_n;h) \coloneqq e^{-\varepsilon^\circ/h}C^{-1}A^\circ u((z',z_n);h)\,,
\]
which is an entire function of $z_n$, holomorphic in $z'$ near $0$. Due to the explicit nature of $A^\circ$, that $u$ is compactly supported and the phase in $A^\circ$ is quadratic, for all $z'$ near $0 = (z^\circ)'$ we have the bound
\[
	e^{-{\Phi^{\flat,\circ}}(z',s)\over h}\left\lvertF(z',s;h)\right\rvert\leq \begin{cases}1 \quad\text{for all}\ s\in {\mathbb{C}}\\ e^{-\varepsilon h^{-1}} \quad\text{for}\ \left\lverts+z_n^\circ\right\rvert\leq \delta' \end{cases}
\]
for some $\varepsilon,\delta>0$ independent of $\varepsilon^\circ$ if $\varepsilon^\circ>0$ is sufficiently small. Note that if $\nu>0$ is chosen sufficiently small, then the circle $\left\lverts+z_n^\circ\right\rvert = \delta$ intersects the negative half of the real line $s^{i{\mathbb{R}}}=0, s^{{\mathbb{R}}}<0$ in two places, so that there are some $s^\circ,\delta > 0$ so that, for $z'$ sufficiently near $0$,
\[
	e^{-{\Phi^{\flat,\circ}}(z',s)\over h}\left\lvertF(z',s;h)\right\rvert\leq \begin{cases}1 \quad\text{for all}\ s\in {\mathbb{C}}\\ e^{-\varepsilon h^{-1}} \quad\text{for}\ \left\lverts+s^\circ\right\rvert\leq \delta \end{cases}
\]

We will apply (the proof of) \cite[Lem.~4.1]{zbMATH05707695} to complete the proof. Define 
\[
	g(z',s) \coloneqq h\log \left\lvertF(z',s;h)\right\rvert 
\]
which satisfies
\[
	g(z',s)-\frac{\hat c}{2}((z')^{\mathbb{R}})^2 \leq \begin{cases}{\hat c\over 2}(s^{\mathbb{R}})^2 \quad&\text{for}\ s^{\mathbb{R}}\geq 0 \\ 0 \quad&\text{for}\ s^{{\mathbb{R}}}\leq 0 \\ -\varepsilon\quad&\text{for}\ \left\lverts+ s^\circ\right\rvert\leq \delta\end{cases}\,.
\]
Notice that the function $f(z',s)\coloneqq {2\over \hat c}g(z',-s)-((z')^{\mathbb{R}})^2$ has the same properties as the function given in the proof of \cite[Lem.~4.1]{zbMATH05707695} that is also denoted by $f$, uniformly for $z'$ near $0$. Following the proof therein, one finds that $f(z',s) \leq -\varepsilon'$, for some $\varepsilon'>0$ as long as $\left\lverts^{\mathbb{R}}\right\rvert\leq \theta_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\left\lverts^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert\leq \theta_{i{\mathbb{R}}}$ for some $\theta_{\mathbb{R}},\theta_{i{\mathbb{R}}}>0$. 
In particular, $g(z',s) \leq -{\hat c\varepsilon'\over 2} + \frac{\hat c}{2}((z')^{\mathbb{R}})^2$ and as in the proof of \cite[Lem.~4.1]{zbMATH05707695}, for $z'$ sufficiently near $0$ we deduce that
\[
	\left\lvertF(z',s;h)\right\rvert = e^{\frac{g(z',s)}{h}}\leq e^{-\frac{\varepsilon''}{h}} 
\]
for some $\varepsilon''>0$ and for $s$ with $\left\lverts^{\mathbb{R}}\right\rvert\leq \theta_{\mathbb{R}}, \left\lverts^{i{\mathbb{R}}}\right\rvert\leq \theta_{i{\mathbb{R}}}$.

In particular, if we choose $\varepsilon^\circ \in (0,\varepsilon'')$ sufficiently small, then we have shown that $A^\circ u =0$ in $\mathbfit{O}^{(\Phi^{\flat,\circ})}_{0}/\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{0}$, which completes the proof.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bproperties}
	Let $\xi'_0\in S^{n-2}$ be arbitrary and fixed. For $a$ from \cref{eq:symbola}, define for $\tau \in {\mathbb{R}}$ near $1$
	\[
		b(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h) \coloneqq (2\pi)^{n-1}a(y',h z_n,h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)a^\ast(y',hz_n,h^{-1}(h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0))\,.
	\]
	and for integers $k\geq 0$ and $\tau$ complex near $1$,
	\[
		b_k(y',z_n,\tau,\eta') \coloneqq (2\pi)^{n-1}\sum_{s+l+j+m=k} \frac{\partial^s_h}{s!}\left(a^\ast_{j}(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)\right)\frac{\partial^m_h}{m!}\left(a_{l}(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0)\right)\Big\vert_{h=0}\,.
	\]
	For $k \geq 1$, $b_k$ is a polynomial of degree $k-1$ in $\eta'$ and a polynomial of degree $k$ in $(\eta',z_n)$ with analytic coefficients and $b_0=(2\pi)^{1-n}$, and each $b_k$ depends holomorphically on $\tau$ near $1$. Furthermore, for every compact $K$ there is $C>0$ so that for every $k\geq 0$ we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundonb_k}
		\sup_{y'\in K}\left\lvertb_k\right\rvert \leq C^{k+1} \sum_{j+m\leq k} j! \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-j-m} \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^m \leq C^{k+1}k! \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^k\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^k_+\,.
	\end{equation}

	Furthermore, for every sufficiently large $C_0>0$ there is $C>0$ so that for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ if $\left\lverthz_n\right\rvert\leq \varepsilon_0$ and $C_0hN \leq 1/2-\varepsilon_0$, we have for $\tau\in {\mathbb{R}}$ near $1$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:diffboundbb_k}
 		\sup_{y'\in K} \left\lvertb(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h)- \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k b_k(y',z_n,\tau,\eta')\right\rvert \leq C^{N+1} h^N\sum_{s+l=0}^N\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^l s! \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert_+^{N-s-l}\,.
	\end{equation}

label: eq:ajtaylork
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall the notation in \cref{eq:symbola}. For any $j\in\mathbb{N}$, by direct computation,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ajtaylork}
		\partial_h^k a_j^\ast(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)\vert_{h=0} = \sum_{l=0}^k {k \choose l} z_n^l (\partial_{y_n}^l (\eta'\cdot \nabla_{\xi'})^{k-l}a_j^\ast)(y',0,\tau\xi'_0)\,.
	\end{equation}
	Recalling the second part of \cref{eq:symbola}, we have
	\[
		((\eta'\cdot \nabla_{\xi'})^{k}a_j^\ast)(y',0,\tau\xi'_0) = \begin{cases} (2\pi)^{1-n}\quad\text{if}\ \ j = k = 0 \\ 0\quad\text{else}\end{cases}\,,\qquad a_j^\ast(y',0,\tau\xi'_0) = (2\pi)^{1-n}\delta_{0j}\,.
	\]
	In particular, \cref{eq:ajtaylork} is a polynomial of degree $\leq k-1$ in $\eta'$ if $k \geq 1$ and identically $(2\pi)^{1-n}$ if $j=k=0$.

	On the other hand,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:otherajtaylor}
		\partial_h^k(a_j(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0))\vert_{h=0} = z_n^k (\partial_{y_n}^ka_j)(y',0,\tau\xi'_0)
	\end{equation}
	is a polynomial of degree $0$ in $\eta'$ for all $j,k\geq 0$ and identically $1$ if $j=k=0$. Thus, by inspecting the explicit formula of $b_k$ we have indeed found that $b_0 = (2\pi)^{-n+1}$ and $b_k$ is a polynomial of degree $\leq k-1$ in $\eta'$ for $k \geq 1$. The holomorphic dependence of $b_k$ on $\tau$ comes from its explicit form and the fact that each $a_j, a_j^\ast$ is holomorphic in the $\eta'$ variable away from the origin. 

	As a direct consequence of Cauchy's inequalities, the bound $\left\lverta_j^\ast(y',0,\tau\xi'_0)\right\rvert \leq C^j j!$, and the explicit formula \cref{eq:ajtaylork} we have (for every compact $K$)
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:easyaastbound}
		\sup_{y'\in K}\left\lvert\partial_h^k a_j^\ast(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert \leq C^{k+j+1} j! k! \sum_{s=0}^k \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^s\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-s}\,.
	\end{equation}
	for some $C>0$ independent of $j,k$. A similar bound holds for \cref{eq:otherajtaylor} which leads to
	\[
		\left\lvertb_k\right\rvert \leq \sum_{s+l+j+m=k} C^{s+j+1} j! C^{l+m+1}\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^m l! \sum_{w=0}^s \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^w \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{s-w}\,.
	\]
	Using \cref{eq:countsum} leads to the first part of \cref{eq:boundonb_k}. (Observe that the sum of the exponents of $j$, $l$, $\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert$, and $\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert$ is always $k$, having bounded $j! \leq j^j, l! \leq l^l$.)
	To obtain the second inequality in \cref{eq:boundonb_k} we merely have to take into account \cref{eq:countsum} a second time.

	We turn now to proving \cref{eq:diffboundbb_k} so that from now on we have $h\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert \leq \varepsilon_0$ and $C_0hN \leq 1/2-\varepsilon_0$ for some sufficiently large $C_0>0$ and $\tau \in {\mathbb{R}}$ near $1$.

	\textbf{Case 1:} $h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \geq \varepsilon_0$.  
	Because $a$ is the holomorphic finite realization of a formal cl.a.s. of order $0$, by \cref{lem:recoversymbol} it is bounded. Thus,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundjustb}
		\left\lvertb(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h)\right\rvert \leq C = Ch^N\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^N (h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert)^{-N} \leq C\varepsilon_0^{-N} h^N \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^N\,.
	\end{equation}
	Furthermore, using \cref{eq:boundonb_k} together with $1 \leq \varepsilon_0^{-j} h^j \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^j$ for all $j\geq 0$ we find that
	\[
		h^k\left\lvertb_k\right\rvert \leq h^N C^{k+1} \sum_{j+m=k} j! \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{N-j-m} \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^m\,.
	\]
	Plugging these two estimates into the calculation
	\[
		\left\lvertb(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h) - \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k b_k(y',z_n,\tau,\eta')\right\rvert \leq \left\lvertb\right\rvert + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k \left\lvertb_k\right\rvert\,,
	\]
	gives \cref{eq:diffboundbb_k} in this case.
	
	\textbf{Case 2:} assume that $h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \leq \varepsilon_0$. This implies that $\left\lvert\eta'+h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0\right\rvert/C_0\geq N$ for $\left\lvert\tau-1\right\rvert< 1/2$ because we had assumed $hC_0N\leq 1/2-\varepsilon_0$. By \cref{eq:symbola} and \cref{lem:recoversymbol} there is $C>0$ so that for all $N\in\mathbb{N}$,
	\[
		a^\ast(y',hz_n,h^{-1}(h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)) = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h^ja^\ast_j(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0) + R_{N,a^\ast}\,,\qquad \left\lvertR_{N,a^\ast}\right\rvert \leq C^{N+1}N!\left\lvert\eta'+h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0\right\rvert^{-N}\,.
	\]
	Using the reverse triangle inequality and $\left\lvert\tau\xi'_0\right\rvert \geq 1/2$ (for $\tau$ near $1$) to write $\left\lvert\eta'+h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0\right\rvert^{-1} = h\left\lverth\eta'+\tau\xi'_0\right\rvert^{-1}\leq h(1/2-\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$, we find
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:rnaastbound}
		\left\lverta^\ast(y',hz_n,h^{-1}(h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)) - \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h^ja^\ast_j(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)\right\rvert \leq C^{N+1} h^N N!\,,
	\end{equation}
	and we have the analogous estimates for $a$.
	At this point, let us write, for any $N\in \mathbb{N}$, 
	\begin{align*}
		b(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h) &= \left(a^\ast(y',hz_n,h^{-1}(h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)) - \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h^j a_j^\ast(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)\right)a(y',hz_n,h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) \\
		&+ \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}h^ja_j^\ast(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0) \left(a(y',hz_n,h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)-\sum_{k=0}^{N-1-j}h^k a_k(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0)\right) \\
		&+ \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h^ja_j^\ast(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0) \sum_{k=0}^{N-1-j} h^ka_k(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0)\,. 
	\end{align*}
	Noting that for some $C>0$ we have $\left\lverta_j^\ast(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0)\right\rvert \leq C^{j+1} j!$ uniformly in all variables because $h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \leq \varepsilon_0 < 1$, using \cref{eq:rnaastbound} (and its analogy for $a$) 
	upon rewriting the last term above, we find 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:firstboundonb}
		\left\lvertb- \sum_{s=0}^{N-1}h^s\sum_{j+k=s}a_j^\ast a_k\right\rvert \leq C^{N+1} h^N N!\,.
	\end{equation}
	We now write
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ajk}
	\begin{aligned}
		a_j^\ast a_k &= a_k\left(a_j^\ast-\sum_{s=0}^{N-j-k-1} h^s \frac{\partial_h^s (a_j^\ast)\vert_{h=0}}{s!}\right) + \sum_{s=0}^{N-j-k-1} h^s \frac{\partial_h^s (a_j^\ast)\vert_{h=0}}{s!} \left(a_k - \sum_{w=0}^{N-j-k-s-1}h^w \frac{\partial_h^w (a_k)\vert_{h=0}}{w!}\right) \\
		&+ \sum_{s=0}^{N-j-k-1} h^s \frac{\partial_h^s (a_j^\ast)\vert_{h=0}}{s!}\sum_{w=0}^{N-j-k-s-1}h^w \frac{\partial_h^w (a_k)\vert_{h=0}}{w!}\,.
	\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Using Taylor's theorem and the Cauchy inequalities with radius $r = \min\{\varepsilon_0\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{-1},\varepsilon_0\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^{-1},\varepsilon_0\}$ (recall $h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \leq \varepsilon_0$ and $h\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert\leq \varepsilon_0$), we have for any $k$,
	\[
		\left\lverta^\ast_j(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0) - \sum_{l=0}^{k-1} \frac{h^l}{l!}\partial_h^l (a^\ast_j(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0))\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert \leq C^{j+1}j! h^k\varepsilon_0^{-k}\sum_{l=0}^{k} \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^l \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-l}\,.
	\]
	Therefore,
	\[
		\left\lverta^\ast_j(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0) - \sum_{l=0}^{N-1-j-k} h^l (l!)^{-1}\partial_h^l (a^\ast_j(y',hz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0))\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert  \leq C^{N+1}j! h^{N-j-k} \sum_{s=0}^{N-j-k}\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^s\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{N-j-k-s}\,.
	\]
	Repeating analogous calculations for $a(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0)$, we find
	\[
		\left\lverta_k(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0) - \sum_{w=0}^{N-1-j-k-s} h^w (w!)^{-1}\partial_h^w (a_k(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0))\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert \leq  C^{N+1}k! h^{N-j-k-s}\sum_{w=0}^{N-j-k-s}\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^w\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{N-j-k-s-w}\,.
	\]
	Using that $\left\lverta_k\right\rvert=\left\lverta_k(y',hz_n,\tau\xi'_0)\right\rvert\leq C^{k+1}k!$ uniformly in all variables as well as the bounds given above, we find that from \cref{eq:ajk} that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ajakbound}
		\left\lverta_j^\ast a_k - \sum_{f=0}^{N-1-j-k} h^f \sum_{s+w=f}\frac{\partial_h^s(a_j^\ast)\vert_{h=0}}{s!}\frac{\partial_h^w (a_k)\vert_{h=0}}{w!}\right\rvert\leq C^{N+1} h^{N-j-k}j!k!\sum_{s+l=0}^{N-j-k} s!\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^l\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{N-j-k-s-l}\,.
	\end{equation}
	Combining \cref{eq:ajakbound,eq:firstboundonb} and recalling the formula of $b_k$ we find \cref{eq:diffboundbb_k}.

label: eq:another_rho
title: Proof
body_md:
Recalling \cref{cor:kerndia}, 
	using Taylor's theorem with remainder of order $1$ (with respect to $z_n$) as well as the homogeneity of $\phi, r^{1/2}$ of degree $1$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:another_rho}
		\rho = -z_n \int_0^1 r^{1/2}(y',shz_n,\partial_{y'}\phi(y',shz_n,\tau\xi'_0)) + r^{1/2}(y',shz_n,\partial_{y'}\phi(y',shz_n,h\eta'+\tau\xi'_0))^\ast \mathrm{d} s
	\end{equation}
	and using the positivity and homogeneity of $r$ we find, for $z_n \geq 0$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhounif}
		\left\lverte^\rho\right\rvert \leq e^{-z_n c(\left\lvert\tau\right\rvert+\left\lverth\eta'+\tau\xi'_0\right\rvert)}
	\end{equation}
	for some $c>0$ uniform in all variables. 

	We proceed to proving the second part of \cref{eq:etabounds}. By \cref{eq:another_rho}, $\rho$ is holomorphic with respect to $h$ at $h=0$ as long as $\left\lverth z_n\right\rvert, \left\lverth \eta'\right\rvert$ are sufficiently small. Working in the separate cases $\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert \leq \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert$ and $\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \leq \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert$, we deduce from the Cauchy inequalities applied to \cref{eq:another_rho} that
	\[
		\sup_{y'\in K}\left\lvert\partial^k_h \rho\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert\leq C^{k}k!\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert (\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^k + \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^k) \leq C^{k}k!\sum_{j=0}^k\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^{j+1}\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-j}
	\]
	for some $C>0$ independent of $k$. Using Fa\`a di Bruno's formula we know that, for $\Pi_k$ the set of partitions of $\{1,\dots,k\}$, for all $k\geq 0$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:faaonrho}
		\partial^k_h e^\rho\vert_{h=0} = e^{\rho}\vert_{h=0} \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} \prod_{B\in\pi} \partial^{\left\lvertB\right\rvert}_h \rho\vert_{h=0}\,,
	\end{equation}
	which together with \cref{eq:another_rho} immediately implies that $\partial_h^ke^\rho\vert_{h=0}$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ in $\eta'$ with analytic coefficients. 

	Furthermore, from \cref{eq:rhounif,eq:faaonrho} we obtain (for $\eta'\neq 0$)
	\[
		\left\lvert\partial_h^k e^{\rho}\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert \leq e^{-z_n c} C^k \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^k \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^{\left\lvert\pi\right\rvert} \prod_{B\in\pi} \left\lvertB\right\rvert!\sum_{j=0}^{\left\lvertB\right\rvert} (\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert/\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert)^j\,,
	\]
	where we used that $\sum_{B\in \pi} \left\lvertB\right\rvert = k$ for any $\pi\in \Pi_k$. Note that for any $i_1,\dots,i_k \geq 0$ with $i_1+\dots+i_k = k$ and any $\zeta\geq 0$ we have
	\[
		\left(\sum_{j=0}^{i_1} \zeta^j\right)\cdots \left(\sum_{j=0}^{i_k} \zeta^j\right) \leq \sum_{j=0}^{k} \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_k \geq 0\\ i_1+\dots+i_k=j}} \zeta^j \leq 4^{k}\sum_{j=0}^k \zeta^j\,,
	\]
	where we used \cref{eq:countsum}. Plugging in $\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{-1}$ for $\zeta$ we find 
	\[
		\left\lvert\partial_h^k e^{\rho}\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert \leq e^{-z_n c}C^{k}4^k \sum_{j=0}^k \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^j \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-j} \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert^{\left\lvert\pi\right\rvert} \prod_{B\in \pi} \left\lvertB\right\rvert!\,.
	\]
	Applying \cref{lem:faabound} completes the proof of \cref{eq:etabounds}.

	To obtain \cref{eq:rhoboundwithint} we apply \cref{eq:etabounds} to find that for any $j,k\geq 0$,
	\[
		\int_0^\infty \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^j \left\lvert\frac{\partial_h^k e^{\rho}}{k!}\vert_{h=0}\right\rvert\mathrm{d} z_n \leq C^{k+1} \sum_{s=0}^k \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-s} \int_0^\infty \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^{j+s} e^{-z_n c}\mathrm{d} z_n\,,
	\]
	and because we identify the Gamma function here, we have
	\[
		 \int_0^\infty \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^{j+s} e^{-z_n c}\mathrm{d} z_n\leq \int_0^\infty (1+z_n^{j+s}) e^{-z_n c}\mathrm{d} z_n = c^{-1} + c^{-1-j-s} (j+s)!\,,
	\]
	which leads to \cref{eq:rhoboundwithint} by applying \cref{eq:sumfac}.


	
	To prove \cref{eq:rhodiffint}, we again make a case distinction. 

	\textbf{Case 1:} We have $h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \geq \varepsilon_0$. First, \cref{eq:rhoboundwithint} implies that
	\[
		\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k \int_0^\infty \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^j\left\lvert\frac{\partial_h^k e^\rho\vert_{h=0}}{k!}\right\rvert \mathrm{d} z_n \leq \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k C^{k+1} j!\sum_{s=0}^k s!\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{k-s} \leq h^N C^{N+1} j!\sum_{s=0}^{N} s! \left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{N-s}\,.
	\]
	On the other hand, \cref{eq:rhounif} implies 
	\[
		\int_0^\infty \left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^j\left\lverte^\rho\right\rvert \left\lvert\chi\right\rvert\mathrm{d} z_n \leq Cj! \leq C^{N+1}j!h^N\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^N\,,
	\]
	for some uniform constant $C>0$. Combining these two estimates gives \cref{eq:rhodiffint} in this case. 

	\textbf{Case 2:} We have $h\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert \leq \varepsilon_0$. Using Taylor's theorem and the Cauchy inequalities we find that
	\[
		\left\lverte^\rho - \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k \frac{\partial_h^k e^\rho\vert_{h=0}}{k!}\right\rvert \leq C^{N+1} h^N e^{-z_n c} \sum_{s=0}^N\left\lvertz_n\right\rvert_+^s\left\lvert\eta'\right\rvert^{N-s}\,,
	\]
	and arguing analogously as for the proof of \cref{eq:rhoboundwithint} we find \cref{eq:rhodiffint}.

Because $b_0 \equiv (2\pi)^{-n+1}$ and the explicit formula for $t_0$ and $\rho\vert_{h=0}$, we find the given expression for $t_0$. 
	Furthermore, \cref{eq:boundsont_kOLD} is a consequence of \cref{eq:boundonb_k,eq:rhoboundwithint}. 

	Performing the substitution $z_n \mapsto hz_n$ in \cref{eq:definet}, we find
	\[
		t(y',\tau,\eta;h) =  h(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^\infty e^{\rho(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h)+ihz_n\eta_n} b(y',z_n,\tau,\eta';h)\chi(hz_n)\mathrm{d} z_n\,.
	\]
	Note that to calculate $t-\sum^{N-1}_{k=0}h^k t_k$ for any $N\in\mathbb{N}$, we write
	\begin{gather*}
		2\pi h^{-1}t \\
		\begin{aligned} &= \int_0^\infty e^{ihz_n\eta_n}\left(e^\rho-\sum^{N-1}_{k=0} h^k \frac{\partial_h^k e^\rho\vert_{h=0}}{k!}\right)b\chi\mathrm{d} z_n + \int_0^\infty e^{ihz_n\eta_n}\sum^{N-1}_{k=0} h^k \frac{\partial_h^k e^\rho\vert_{h=0}}{k!}\left(b-\sum_{j=0}^{N-k-1}h^jb_j\right)\chi\mathrm{d} z_n \\

		&+\int_0^\infty \sum^{N-1}_{k=0} h^k\frac{\partial_h^k e^\rho\vert_{h=0}}{k!}\sum_{j=0}^{N-k-1}h^jb_j \left(e^{ihz_n\eta_n} - \sum_{l=0}^{N-k-j-1}h^l \frac{(iz_n\eta_n)^l}{l!}\right)\mathrm{d} z_n\,.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{gather*}
	The fourth term is equal to $(2\pi)\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h^k t_k$ after reordering and one may use the bounds \cref{eq:rhodiffint,eq:boundonb_k} (and writing $b= b-b_0+b_0$) to bound the first term, \cref{eq:diffboundbb_k,eq:rhoboundwithint} to bound the second term and the first part of \cref{eq:boundonb_k}, and \cref{eq:etabounds} and \cref{eq:rhoboundwithint} to bound the third term, as well as Taylor's theorem and \cref{eq:boundonb_k,eq:rhoboundwithint} to bound the last term to obtain \cref{eq:diffboundt}. 

	To prove the homogeneity of each $t_k$ we proceed as follows: using \cref{eq:definet}, for any $s$ real near $1$, we have $h^{-1} t(y',s\tau,\eta;h) = h^{-1}t(y',\tau,\eta;h/s) = s^{-1} (h/s)^{-1} t(y',\tau,\eta;h/s)$, so that expanding the LHS in terms of $t_k$ and the RHS in terms of $t_k$, we obtain the formal sums $\sum_{k\geq 0} h^k t_k(y',s\tau,\eta)$ and $\sum_{k\geq 0} h^k s^{-k-1} t_k(y,\tau,\eta)$ respectively, and the uniqueness of asymptotic (Poincar\'e) expansions implies that $s^{-k-1} t_k(y,\tau,\eta) = t_k(y',s\tau,\eta)$ for real $s$ near $1$ and all $k$. Since however, both terms are holomorphic with respect to $s$, this equality extends to complex $s$.
