title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tilde{q}\in C^\omega(U)$. We know from \cref{eq:boundsont_k} that for every $k\geq 0$, $\mathrm{Op}^R(t_k)\tilde{q} = \sum_{j=0}^k \mathrm{Op}^R(t_{k,j})\tilde{q}$, where $t_{k,j}$ is a polynomial of degree $j$ in $\eta$ bounded uniformly in $y'$ above by $C^{k+1}(k-j)!\left\lvert\eta\right\rvert^j$. Furthermore, because $\mathrm{Op}^R(t_k)\tilde{q}$ is a differential operator of order $k$ with analytic coefficients acting on $\tilde{q}$ by \cref{prop:allthingst}, for some $C>0$ and all $k\in\mathbb{N}$
	\[
		\left\lvert\mathrm{Op}^R(t_k)\tilde{q}\right\rvert \leq \sum_{j=0}^k C^{k+1} (k-j)! C^{j+1} j! \leq C^{2k+2} (k+1)! \leq (3C)^{2k} k!\,,
	\]
	in a complex neighborhood of $(0,1)$ (with respect to $x,\tau$), so that we have indeed shown that $\sum_{k\geq 0} h^k \mathrm{Op}^R(t_k)\tilde{q}\vert_{x_n=0}$ is a formal cl.a.s. near $(0,1)$ (with respect to $x',\tau$).

	According to \cref{eq:sigmaist}, when $\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}$ is near $1$, we have
	\[
		\sigma_b^{\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)= T(\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q})(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) = \iint e^{i(x'-y)\cdot\eta} t(y',\tau,\eta;h) \tilde{q}(y)\mathrm{d}\eta \mathrm{d} y\,.  
	\]
	Now relying on \cref{eq:tpolybound} together with the Cauchy inequalities and using that $\tilde{q}\in C_c^\infty$, for $j$ sufficiently large, 
	\[
		\left\lvert\iint e^{i(x'-y)\cdot\eta}\left(t - h\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}h^k t_k\right)\tilde{q} \mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d} y\right\rvert = \left\lvert\iint e^{i(x'-y)\cdot\eta}(1+\left\lvert\eta\right\rvert^2)^{-j}(1+\Delta_y)^j\left(\left(t - h\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}h^k t_k\right)\tilde{q}\right) \mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d} y\right\rvert = \mathcal{O}(h^{N+1})\,.
	\]
	Recall from \cref{prop:symbcalc}, for $(x',\tau)$ real near $(0,1)$,
	\[
		(\sigma_a^{\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}-\sigma_b^{\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}})(x',h^{-1}\tau \xi'_0) = \mathcal{O}_M(h^M)
	\]
	for all $M$. By \cref{prop:direc1}, we may expand $\sigma_a^{\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}\sim h\sum_{k\geq 0}h^k\sigma_k$ for some $\sigma_k$, and since (Poincar\'e) asymptotic expansions of functions are unique (\cite[\S~2.1(iii)]{NIST:DLMF}, \cite{zbMATH00994432}), we have shown that for real $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$ we have
	\[
		\sigma_k = \mathrm{Op}^R(t_k)\tilde{q}\,.
	\]
	Furthermore, because both the LHS and RHS above are holomorphic functions of $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$, and their restrictions to a real open neighborhood of $(0,1)$ align, they must coincide for complex $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$ (see for example \cite[Thm.~3.1.15]{hoermander1}).

label: thm:foundtdq
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:foundtdq}
	Let $\xi'_0\in S^{n-2}$ be fixed arbitrarily and $\tau\in {\mathbb{C}}$ sufficiently near $1$. For every $q\in L^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ supported in $\{y_n \geq 0\}$ for which $\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)$ is a cl.a.s. of order $-1$ (in $h>0$, depending holomorphically on $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$), there is $\tilde{q}\in C_c^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ that is analytic near $0$ so that $\sigma_a^{q-\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)$ is a holomorphic function of $(x',\tau)$ on an open complex neighborhood of $(0,1)$ so that  
	\[
		\sigma_a^{q-\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) \in \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,.
	\]

label: eq:clasexp
title: Proof
body_md:
According to our assumption we can write, for some $\sigma_k$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:clasexp}
		h^{-1}\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) \sim \sum_{k\geq 0}h^k \sigma_k(x',\tau\xi'_0)\,.
	\end{equation}
	Because $\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)$ is a function of $\tau/h$, for real $s$ near $1$, $h^{-1}\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}s\tau\xi'_0) = s^{-1}(h/s)^{-1}\sigma_a^q(x',(h/s)^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)$, so that expanding both of these expressions in powers of $h$ (using \cref{eq:clasexp}), one obtains homogeneity of degree $k+1$ of each $\sigma_k(x',h^{-1}s\tau\xi'_0)$ for real $s$ near $1$, which due to holomorphicity and the identity theorem is upgraded to the desired homogeneity: $\sigma_k(x',\tau) = \tau^{-k-1}\sigma_k(x',1)$ for all complex $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$ and all $k$.

	We seek $\tilde{q}$ of the form
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:tdq}
		\tilde{q}(x) = \chi(x)\sum_{k\geq 0} q_k(x';\xi'_0)\frac{x_n^k}{k!}\,,
	\end{equation}
	where $\chi \in C_c^\infty$ is identically $1$ near $0$, and we want 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:whatwewant}
		\mathrm{Op}^{R}(t_k)\tilde{q}(x',0) = \tau^{-k-1}\sigma_k(x',\xi'_0) = \sigma_k(x',\tau\xi'_0)
	\end{equation}
	for all $k\geq 0$. Note that if $\tau$ is real and near $1$, then $t_k$ is homogeneous of degree $-k-1$ in $\tau$ by \cref{prop:allthingst}. In particular, if we obtain	    
	\[
		\mathrm{Op}^{R}(t_k)\tilde{q}(x',0)\vert_{\tau =1} = \sigma_k(x',\xi'_0)
	\]
	then by virtue of the homogeneity we have \cref{eq:whatwewant} for $\tau$ real near $1$ and because both the LHS and RHS are holomorphic in $\tau$ near $1$ we will then have it for all complex $\tau$ near $1$. Thus we restrict to $\tau = 1$. 

	Because $t_0 =(2\pi)^{-n}(2r^{1/2}(y',0,\tau\xi'_0))^{-1}$, define (the factor $(2\pi)^{-n}$ disappears due to Fourier inversion when applying $\mathrm{Op}^R(t_0)$)
	\[
		q_0(x';\xi'_0) = 2 r^{1/2}(x',0,\xi'_0)\sigma_0(x';\xi'_0)\,.
	\]
	We use the explicit formula for $t_k$ from \cref{eq:tkformula}: (which uses that $b_0=(2\pi)^{-n+1}$ and $e^{\rho}\vert_{h=0}$ is explicit too)
	\[
		\mathrm{Op}^R(t_k) = (2r^{1/2}(x',0,\xi'_0))^{-k-1}\partial_{x_n}^k + \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \partial_{x_n}^j P_{k,j}(x',D';\xi'_0)\,,
	\]
	where $P_{k,j}$ are differential operators of order $k-j$ in $y'$ with analytic coefficients.  
	We want the RHS above when applied to $\tilde{q}$ and evaluated at $(x',0)$ to equal $\sigma_k(x',\xi'_0)$, so we inductively define
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:qkdef}
		q_k(x';\xi'_0) \coloneqq (2r^{1/2}(x',0,\xi'_0))^{k+1}\left(\sigma_k(x';\xi'_0)- \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \partial_{x_n}^j P_{k,j}(x',D';\xi'_0)\sum_{s=0}^{k-1} q_s(x')\frac{x_n^s}{s!}\vert_{x_n=0}\right)\,.
	\end{equation}
	Noting that according to \cref{eq:boundsont_k}, we can write $\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \partial_{x_n}^j P_{k,j} = \sum_{j=0}^k \tilde{P}_{k,j}$, where each $\tilde{P}_{k,j}$ is a differential operator of order $j$ with analytic coefficients bounded by $C^{k+1}(k-j)!$, we deduce (by an inductive argument) that each $q_k$ defined according to \cref{eq:qkdef} is analytic in $x'$ and satisfies $\left\lvert\partial^\alpha q_k\right\rvert \leq C^{\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert+k+1}\alpha!k!$ (with $C>0$ independent of $k$). In particular, defining $\tilde{q}$ according to \cref{eq:tdq} and choosing the support of $\chi$ therein sufficiently small to guarantee convergence of the series, $\tilde{q}$ is analytic near $x=0$ and (modulo the cut-off $\chi$) uniquely determined by the choices of $q_k$ we have made.

	Because $\chi$ in $\tilde{q}$ is identically $1$ near the origin, we have achieved that 
	\[
		h^{-1}\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)\sim \sum_{k\geq 0} h^k\sigma_k(x',\tau\xi'_0) = \sum_{k\geq 0}h^k\mathrm{Op}^{R}(t_k)\tilde{q}(x',0)\,.
	\]
	Now, \cref{prop:sigmatotq} states that  
	\[
		h^{-1}\sigma_a^{\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) \sim \sum_{k\geq 0}h^k\mathrm{Op}^{R}(t_k)\tilde{q}(x',0)\,,
	\]
	which is to say that for complex $(x',\tau)$ sufficiently near $(0,1)$,
	\[
		\sigma_a^{q- \mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)=\sigma_a^q(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) - \sigma_a^{\mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) \sim 0\,.
	\]
	At first, the term on the LHS is \emph{a priori} merely a distribution (well-defined since the support of the argument is in $y_n\geq 0$) in space parametrized by $\tau\xi'_0$, but nevertheless the term in the middle is the finite realization of the formal cl.a.s. $0$, which by definition of cl.a.s. gives the desired exponential decay.

body_md:
The implication 2.$\implies$ 1. of this statement was shown in \cref{prop:direc1}. According to \cref{prop:sigmatotq} we know that $\sigma_a^{1_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q}}$ has lowest order term
	\[
		\mathrm{Op}(t_0)\tilde{q}(x',0) = (2r^{1/2}(x',0,\tau\xi'_0))^{-1}\tilde{q}(x',0)\,,
	\]
	which is non-vanishing near $(0,1)$ if and only if $\tilde{q}(0) \neq 0$. We turn to proving that 1. $\implies$ 2.

    We first reduce to the case that $q \in L^\infty(M)$ is supported sufficiently close to $\hat y = 0$. Choose $\chi_1 \in C_c^\infty(M)$ identically $1$ near $\hat y$ and supported sufficiently close to $\hat y$. The kernel 
    \[
        \dot\Lambda_{(1-\chi_1)q}(x',z') = -\int_M (1-\chi_1(y))q(y)K(y,x')K(y,z')\mathrm{d} V_g(y) 
    \] 
    is jointly analytic near $(0,0)$ because the Poisson kernels are integrated only where they are analytic. In particular, by the contour formula given in \cref{prop:anasymb} for $\sigma_a^{(1-\chi_1)q}$, a contour deformation using Stokes' theorem to the contour $\tilde{\gamma}_{\xi'}(t') = t'+ir\xi'_0$ shows that $\sigma_a^{(1-\chi_1)q}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) \in \mathbfit{O}_{(0,1)}^{(-\omega)}$. As a consequence, $\sigma_a^{\chi_1 q}$ is a cl.a.s. of order $-1$ for $(x',\tau)$ near $(0,1)$.

    Now choose $\tilde{q}$ according to \cref{thm:foundtdq} applied to $\sigma_a^{\chi_1 q}$ and denote 
    \[
        u  = \mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q} - q = \mathbb{1}_{\{y_n\geq 0\}}\tilde{q} - \chi_1 q - (1-\chi_1)q\,,
    \]
    so that $\sigma^u_a(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0)\in \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}$. 

	For $(\tilde{\chi}_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ an Ehrenpreis cut-off sequence identically $1$ and supported near $0$, for $j_\vartheta$ from \cref{prop:K2}, and $\chi_0 \in C_c^\infty(\partial M)$ identically $1$ near $0$ and $\mathrm{supp} \chi_0 \subset \{\tilde{\chi}_j \equiv 1\forall j\}$, define
	\[
		g_{\tau,h}(z') = \tilde{\chi}_{j_\vartheta(h)}(z')e^{\frac{i}{h}\tau z'\cdot\xi'_0}\,,\quad f_{v',\tau,h}(x') = \chi_0(x')e^{\frac{i}{h}\left( \frac{i}{2}(v'-x')^2+\frac{i}{2}(\tau-1)^2+x'\cdot\xi'_0\right)}\,,
	\]
    Because $\tilde{q}$ is analytic near the origin, using \cref{prop:direc1} and the assumption on $\dot\Lambda_q$, we know that $\dot\Lambda_u$ is analytic off the diagonal near the origin which allows us to apply \cref{prop:anasymb}: for $\vartheta>0$ sufficiently small we have
	\[
		-\dot\Lambda_u g_{\tau,h} = e^{\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}\sigma_a^{u}(x',h^{-1}\tau\xi'_0) + e^{\frac{i}{h}\tau x'\cdot\xi'_0}\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)} =  \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,.
	\]
	Let $\chi\in C_c^\infty$ be a cut-off supported sufficiently close to $0$ and identically $1$ near $0$. The kernel $\dot\Lambda_{(1-\chi)u}$ is analytic near $(0,0)$ because the two Poisson kernels in its definition are separated from the diagonal, and we may assume that $\mathrm{supp} \chi_j$ is a subset of this neighborhood of analyticity for all $j$. In particular, we may use repeated partial integrations to find that, for $\vartheta>0$ sufficiently small, 
	\[
		\dot\Lambda_{(1-\chi)u} g_{\tau,h} \in \mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,.
	\]
	Because $\dot\Lambda_u g_{\tau,h} = \dot\Lambda_{\chi u} g_{\tau,h} + \dot\Lambda_{(1-\chi)u} g_{\tau,h}$, we find that, using \cref{cor:Ks} and \cref{eq:defofS}, 
	\[
		\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\ni \langle\dot\Lambda_{\chi u} g_{\tau,h},f_{v',\tau,h}\rangle = -\int \chi u Kg_{\tau,h} \overline{Kf_{v',\tau,h}}\mathrm{d} V_g = S_{-\xi'_0}(\chi u)(v',\tau;h)+\mathbfit{O}^{(-\omega)}_{(0,1)}\,.
	\]
	Choosing the support of $\chi$ sufficiently small, \cref{cor:vanish} implies that $\chi u$, and thus $u$, vanishes near the origin which completes the proof.

After dividing the desired estimate by $r^m$, we may assume that $m=0$. After replacing $r$ by $r\left\lvert\xi\right\rvert$ and $\xi$ by $\xi\left\lvert\xi\right\rvert^{-1}$, by modifying $C,C_0>0$ we may assume that $K \subset \{\left\lvert\xi\right\rvert=1\}$.

	Since $N \leq r/C_0$, if $C_0$ is sufficiently large,
	\[
		p(x,r\xi)-\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} r^{-k}p_k(x,\xi) = p(x,r\xi) - \sum_{k\leq r/C_0} r^{-k} p_k(x,\xi) + \sum_{N \leq k\leq r/C_0} r^{-k}p_k(x,\xi)
	\]
	where the difference of the first two terms is bounded above in absolute value by $Ce^{-\varepsilon r}$ for some $C,\varepsilon>0$. By standard estimates (\cite[Eq.~(1.2.16)]{doi:10.1142/1550}) we have
	\[
		e^{-\varepsilon r} \leq \varepsilon^{-N} N^{N} r^{-N} \leq (e\varepsilon^{-1})^{N} r^{-N} N!\,.
	\]
	For the second term we estimate
	\begin{align*}
		\left\lvert\sum_{N \leq k\leq r/C_0} r^{-k}p_k\right\rvert &\leq \sum_{N \leq k\leq r/C_0} r^{-k}C^kk! = \sum_{0\leq k\leq r/C_0-N} r^{-k-N}C^{k+N}(k+N)!\\
		&= r^{-N} (2C)^N N! \sum_{0\leq k\leq r/C_0-N} (2Ck/r)^k \leq r^{-N}(2C)^N N! \sum_{0\leq k\leq r/C_0-N} e^{-k}\,,
	\end{align*}
	where we used the estimates $(k+N)! \leq 2^{k+N} k! N! \leq 2^{k+N}N! k^k$. The last inequality is provided $C_0>2Ce$ is large enough. Then we may bound
	\[
		\sum_{0\leq k\leq r/C_0-N} e^{-k} \leq \sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{-k} \leq \frac{1}{1-e^{-1}}\,,
	\]
	so that we indeed find \cref{eq:RNerr}.

label: lem:faabound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:faabound}
	Let $x \geq 0, k\in \mathbb{N}, k\geq 1$ and $\Pi_k$ be the set partitions of $\{1,\dots,k\}$. We have
	\[
		\sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} x^{\left\lvert\pi\right\rvert}\prod_{B\in\pi}\left\lvertB\right\rvert! \leq 4^{k}\sum_{j=0}^k x^{k-j}j!\,.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define $f(y) = e^{(y-1)x}$ and $g(y) = \frac{1}{1-y} = \sum_{k\geq 0}y^k$ for $\left\lverty\right\rvert<1$. We have $\partial^n_y g(0)=n!$ and $\partial^n_y f(1)=x^n$ for all $n\geq 0$. By Fa\`a di Bruno's formula (first the combinatorial version, then the (equivalent) one using Bell polynomials $B_{k,j}$),
	\[
		\partial^k (f\circ g)(0)= \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} x^{\left\lvert\pi\right\rvert}\prod_{B\in\pi}\left\lvertB\right\rvert! = \sum_{j=1}^k x^j B_{k,j}(1!,2!,\dots,(k-j+1)!)\,.
	\]
	According to \cite[\S~3.3~Thm.~B]{zbMATH03443655}, $B_{k,j}(1!,2!,\dots,(k-j+1)!) = {k-1 \choose j-1}\frac{k!}{j!}$, which are called the Lah numbers. 

	Changing variables $m = k-j$, and using 
	\[
		{k-1 \choose j-1}\frac{k!}{j!} = {k \choose m}{k-1\choose m}m! \leq 2^k 2^{k-1} m! \leq 4^k m!\,, 
	\]
	we have
	\[
		\sum_{\pi \in \Pi_k} x^{\left\lvert\pi\right\rvert}\prod_{B\in\pi}\left\lvertB\right\rvert! = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} x^{k-j} {k \choose j}{k-1\choose j}j! \leq 4^k \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} x^{k-j}j!\,,
	\]
	which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
The basic properties of the spectrum of the Dirichlet realization of $L$ follow from \cite[Thm.~1.7.2]{zbMATH00857699}, see also \cite[Chp.~2~\S~9]{MR350177}. We shall invoke \cite{zbMATH01346906} to prove the statements 1. and 2., for which we shall provide some set-up. The G\aa{}rding inequality, see \cite[Thm.~1.7.2]{zbMATH00857699}, implies there is some constant $b>0$ so that the form (defined initially on $C_c^\infty(M^{\mathrm{int}})$)
    \[
        A(u,v) \coloneqq \langle Lu, v\rangle_{L^2(M)} + b \langle u,v\rangle_{L^2(M)}
    \]
    extends continuously to a positive closed form on $H_0^{m/2}(M)$, and defines an equivalent norm to $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{H^{m/2}}$. 

    For every smooth open $U\subset M$, denote by $D_U$ the closure in $H_0^{m/2}(M)$ of the zero extension to $M$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(U)$, so that $D_U$ can be identified with $H^{m/2}_0(U)$. The operator corresponding to the restriction of the form $A$ to $D_U$ is $L_U+b$, where $L_U$ is the Dirichlet realization of $L$ on $H^m(U) \cap H^{m/2}_0(U)$. 
    
    By the Rellich-Kondrachov embedding theorem \cite[Thm.~2.34]{MR1636569}, the embedding of $D_U$ into $L^2(U)$ is compact, and if $U_1\subset U_2$, then $D_{U_1} \subset D_{U_2}$ for any smooth open $U_1, U_2 \subset M$, and if $D_{U_1}=D_{U_2}$, then we must have $U_1 = U_2$. If $(W_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}}, W$ are according to 2. in the statement, the union $\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty D_{W_j}$ is dense in $D_W$: every function $\in C_c^\infty(W)$ is supported in some $W_j$. Thus, the statements 1. and 2. are consequences of \cite{zbMATH01346906} after subtracting the common shift $b$ from the eigenvalues. 
    
    The proof of statement 3. under the additional unique continuation assumption follows the proof of \cite[Thm.~2.3]{zbMATH03393073} almost verbatim, see also the proof of \cite[Prop.~C.3]{busch2025generalizedboundaryrigidityminimal}, and we shall not reiterate it.

label: cor:perturbDEV
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:perturbDEV}
    In the setting of \cref{thm:DEV}, assuming that $L$ satisfies the unique continuation property therein, if $M' \subset M$ is some connected open set with $C^{\infty}$ boundary so that $L$ has Dirichlet eigenvalue $0$ restricted to $M'$, for any $x \in \overline{M'}$ and open neighborhood $W$ of $x$ in $\overline{M'}$, there is some open neighborhood $U\subset W$ of $x$ so that $M'\setminus \bar U$ is connected, has $C^{\infty}$ boundary and $L$ does not have Dirichlet eigenvalue $0$ restricted to $M'\setminus \bar U$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $\lambda_k(M') = 0$ and $\lambda_i(M') < 0$ for all $i < k$, i.e., $\lambda_k(M')$ is the first zero Dirichlet eigenvalue. Let $U_j \subset W, j\in\mathbb{N}$ be a sequence of bounded open neighborhoods of $x$ with smooth boundary so that $\bigcap_{j \geq 1} U_j = \{x\}$, $U_{j+1} \subset U_{j}$, $U_{j}\setminus \bar U_{j+1}$ contains and open set and $M'\setminus \bar U_j$ is connected for every $j$. Define $\Omega_j = M'\setminus \bar U_j$, and note that strict monotonicity of eigenvalues gives $\lambda_k(\Omega_j) > 0$ for all $j$, which completes the proof if $k=1$: choose $U = U_1$, say.

    If, however, $k>1$, because $\lambda_k(\Omega_j)>0$ for any $j$, if $i\in \mathbb{N}$ so that $\lambda_i(\Omega_j)=0$, we must have $i < k$. Thus consider the following list of $k-1$ different sequences 
    \[
        (\lambda_1(\Omega_j))_{j\in\mathbb{N}}, \dots, (\lambda_{k-1}(\Omega_j))_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\,.
    \]
    Strict monotonicity of eigenvalues implies that each of these sequences is strictly decreasing, so that there is some $j^\circ$ sufficiently large so that 
    \[
        \lambda_1(\Omega_{j^\circ})\neq 0, \dots, \lambda_{k-1}(\Omega_{j^\circ}) \neq 0\,,
    \]
    for if, say $\lambda_i(\Omega_j)=0$ for some $i,j$, we must have $\lambda_i(\Omega_{j+1})>0$. Since $\lambda_{l}(\Omega_{j^\circ}) \geq \lambda_k(\Omega_{j^\circ})>0$ for all $l\geq k$, the proof is complete by choosing $U= U_{j^\circ}$.

title: Remark
body_md: The unique continuation property imposed on $L$ in \cref{thm:DEV} is automatically true if $m=2$ by the usual unique continuation statements (\cite{zbMATH03174689}, \cite[\S~17.2]{zbMATH05129478}). On the other hand, this is also true if $L$ has analytic coefficients in $M$ without any restriction on its order (\cite[Thm.~8.6.1]{hoermander1}). Note also that it suffices to require that the sets $U, U_1, U_2, W_j, W$ in \cref{thm:DEV} have $C^{1,1}$ boundary if $m=2$.

label: prop:GK
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:GK}
	Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. Let $L$ be a strongly elliptic formally self-adjoint differential operator with smooth coefficients on $M$ of even order $m$. If $L$ does not have Dirichlet eigenvalue $0$ (restricted to $M$), the Green's and Poisson operators $G$ and $K$ are well-defined and for every $s\geq m$
	\[
		G \colon H^{s-m}(M) \to H^{s}(M)\cap H^{m/2}_0(M)\,,\qquad K \colon \prod_{j=0}^{m/2-1} H^{s-j-\frac{1}{2}}(\partial M) \to H^s(M)
	\]
	are continuous. Here, $G, K$ are uniquely determined by the property that 
    \[
        LG u = u\,, \quad (\partial_\nu^j Gu\vert_{\partial M})_{j=0}^{m/2-1} = 0\,, \qquad \forall u \in H^{s-m}(M)\,,
    \]
    and
    \[
            LK g = 0\,, \quad (\partial_\nu^j Kg\vert_{\partial M})_{j=0}^{m/2-1} = g\,, \qquad \forall g \in \prod_{j=0}^{m/2-1} H^{s-j-\frac{1}{2}}(\partial M)\,.
    \]

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of \cite[Prop.~A.2]{zbMATH07203082} we take arbitrary $F \in (H^s(U))^\ast$ satisfying $\langle F,Kf\vert_U \rangle = 0$ for all $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)^{m/2}$. By the Hahn-Banach theorem, proving that $\langle F, u \rangle = 0$ for all $u\in\mathcal{S}$ completes the proof. 

	We first extend $F$ to $\hat F \in (H^s(M))^\ast$ as $\langle \hat F,u\rangle \coloneqq \langle F, u\vert_U\rangle$ for all $u\in H^s(M)$. Furthermore, invoking \cref{prop:GK}, we define
	\[
		\varphi \in (H^{s-m}(M))^\ast\,,\quad \langle \varphi, h\rangle \coloneqq \langle \hat F, G h\rangle \quad \forall h\in H^{s-m}(M)\,,
	\]
	and
	\[
		\rho \in \prod_{j=0}^{m/2-1} (H^{s-j-1/2}(\partial M))^\ast = \prod_{j=0}^{m/2-1} H^{-(s-j-1/2)}(\partial M)\,, \quad \langle \rho, g \rangle \coloneqq \langle \hat F, Kg\rangle\quad\forall g\in \prod_{j=0}^{m/2-1} H^{s-j-1/2}(\partial M)\,.
	\]
	Defining the trace map $\gamma\colon H^s(M) \ni u \mapsto (\partial_\nu^0 u\vert_{\partial M},\dots, \partial_\nu^{m/2-1} u\vert_{\partial M})\in \prod_{j=0}^{m/2-1} H^{s-j-1/2}(\partial M)$, any $u \in H^s(M)$ can be written $u = u - K(\gamma u) + K(\gamma u) = u_0 + K(\gamma u)$ with $GL u_0 = u_0$. In particular,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:imp}
		\langle \hat F, u\rangle = \langle \hat F, u_0 \rangle + \langle \hat F, K(\gamma u)\rangle = \langle \varphi, Lu_0\rangle + \langle \rho, \gamma u\rangle =  \langle \varphi, Lu\rangle + \langle \rho, \gamma u\rangle\,,\quad \forall u \in H^s(M)\,,
	\end{equation}
	where we used the definitions of $\varphi, \rho$ and that $L K = 0$. Now by assumption, for all $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)^{m/2}$, 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:imp2}
		0 = \langle F, Kf\vert_U\rangle = \langle \hat F, Kf\rangle = \langle \rho, f\rangle\,,\quad \text{so that}\quad \rho\vert_{\Gamma} = 0\,,
	\end{equation}
	(or more precisely, $\rho\vert_{\Gamma^{m/2}} = 0$).

	Introduce some compact manifold $N$ without boundary so that $N\supset M$ and extend $\varphi$ as $\tilde{\varphi}$ to $(H^{s-m}(N))^\ast = H^{m-s}(N)$ (\cite[\S~4~Prop.~3.2]{zbMATH05771951}) defined by $\langle \tilde{\varphi}, \psi \rangle_{N} = \langle \varphi, \psi\vert_M\rangle$ for all $\psi \in H^{s-m}(N)$. We also extend $L$ elliptically with smooth coefficients to $N$ as $\tilde{L}$. We will show that $\mathrm{supp} \varphi \subset \bar U \cup (\partial M\setminus \Gamma)$: for all $\psi \in C_c^\infty(N)$ so that $\mathrm{supp} \psi \cap \bar U = \emptyset$ and $\mathrm{supp} \psi\vert_{\partial M} \subset \Gamma$, from \cref{eq:imp,eq:imp2} we conclude
	\[
		\langle \tilde{L}^\ast \tilde{\varphi}, \psi \rangle_{N} = \langle \tilde{\varphi}, \tilde{L}\psi\rangle_{N} = \langle \varphi, L\psi\rangle = \langle \hat F, \psi\rangle - \langle \rho, \gamma \psi\rangle = 0\,,
	\]
	where we also used that $\mathrm{supp} \hat F \subset \bar U$. Therefore, elliptic regularity for $\tilde{L}$ (\cite[Cor.~8.3.2]{hoermander1}) implies that $\tilde{\varphi} \in C^\infty(N \setminus (\bar U \cup (\partial M\setminus \Gamma)))$, which implies that $\tilde{\varphi}$ is smooth in an open neighborhood of $\Gamma_0 \subset \partial M$ in $N$ and we know $\tilde{\varphi}$ vanishes in $N\setminus M$. We conclude that $\varphi \in C^\infty((M^{\mathrm{int}}\setminus \bar U)\cup \Gamma_0)$ satisfies $L^\ast \varphi = 0$ in $M^{\mathrm{int}}\setminus \bar U$ and $\partial_\nu^j \varphi\vert_{\Gamma_0} = 0\forall j\geq 0$ so that the unique continuation assumption implies that $\varphi$ vanishes in $M^{\mathrm{int}}\setminus \bar U$. 

	Denote by $\Gamma' \supset \bar U \cap \partial M$ some non-empty open subset of $\partial M$ so that $\Gamma' \subset \Gamma \cup ((\partial M \cap \bar U)\setminus \Xi)$. Given arbitrary $u\in\mathcal{S}$, there is an open $W\supset \bar U$ (with respect to the topology on $M$) with $W\cap \partial M \subset \Gamma'$ and an extension $\hat u \in H^s(M)$ of $u$ so that $\mathrm{supp} \hat u \subset W$.  
	In particular, $\mathrm{supp} \gamma \hat u\vert_{\partial M} \subset \Gamma'$. By assumption on $u$ and the fact that $\hat u$ extends $u$, we know that $\gamma \hat u \vert_{(\bar U \cap \partial M)\setminus \Xi} = 0$, which combined with \cref{eq:imp2} (and the fact that $\Gamma' \subset \Gamma \cup ((\partial M \cap \bar U)\setminus \Xi)$) implies $\langle \rho, \gamma \hat u\rangle = 0$.

	Thus, \cref{eq:imp} implies
	\[
		\langle F, u \rangle_U = \langle \hat F, \hat u\rangle = \langle \varphi, L\hat u\rangle = \langle \varphi\vert_W, L\hat u\vert_W\rangle_W\,.
	\]
	Recall that $\mathrm{supp} \varphi \subset \bar U \cup (\partial M \setminus \Gamma)$ and because $W$ was chosen so that
	\[
		W\cap \partial M \subset \Gamma' \subset \Gamma \cup ((\partial M \cap \bar U)\setminus \Xi) = \Gamma \cup (\partial M \cap \bar U)\,,
	\]
	we have $\mathrm{supp} \varphi\vert_W \subset \bar U$, so that we may interpret $\varphi\vert_W$ as an element of $H^{m-s}_{\bar U}(N) = \{v \in H^{m-s}(N)\colon \mathrm{supp} v \subset \bar U\}$, so that according to \cite[Thm.~3.29]{zbMATH01446717} there are some $\varphi_j \in C_c^\infty(U)$ so that $\varphi_j \to \varphi\vert_W$ as $j\to \infty$ in $H^{m-s}(N)$. We thus have
	\[
		\langle F, u \rangle_U = \langle \varphi\vert_W, L\hat u\vert_W\rangle_W = \lim_{j\to\infty}\langle \varphi_j, L \hat u\rangle_N = \lim_{j\to\infty}\langle \varphi_j, L u\rangle_U = 0\,,
	\]
	completing the proof.
